title: Unconditional Security of Discrete-Modulated CV-QKD from Infinite-Dimensional MEAT
summary: Discrete-Modulated (DM) Continuous-Variable (CV) Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is an experimentally attractive approach to quantum cryptography, offering high key rates over metropolitan-scale distances while relying on state-of-the-art telecom infrastructure. However, a fundamental gap has remained between this experimental promise and rigorous security: for more than two decades, DM CV-QKD has lacked a complete composable finite-size security proof against coherent attacks. Existing works either restrict the adversary to collective attacks, impose additional finite-dimensional assumptions, apply only to specific modulation formats, or fail to recover the known asymptotic rates. Here, we resolve this longstanding problem by establishing the first complete composable finite-size security proof for DM CV-QKD protocols against coherent attacks, incorporating imperfect detectors and both fixed- and variable-length protocol variants. Our proof introduces two central results of broader interest: an infinite-dimensional marginal-constrained entropy accumulation theorem (iMEAT) and a rigorous dimension-reduction technique that makes the infinite-dimensional security bounds numerically tractable. The resulting key rates recover the known asymptotic rates and outperform established finite-size bounds based on collective attacks, while yielding positive key rates beyond $70$km for experimentally relevant block sizes and parameters. Thus, our work closes a longstanding gap and places an experimentally attractive class of CV-QKD protocols on a rigorous composable security footing and provides a pathway towards their practical deployment.

AI.motivation: DM CV-QKD is experimentally attractive, offering high key rates over metropolitan distances using standard telecom infrastructure, but for over two decades it lacked a complete composable finite-size security proof against coherent attacks. Prior works restricted the adversary to collective attacks, imposed finite-dimensional assumptions, applied only to specific modulation formats, or failed to recover asymptotic rates.

title: Direct Observation of Dipolar-Driven Anisotropic Quantum Projection Noise in a Solid-State Spin Ensemble
summary: The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond is a prominent quantum-sensing platform. Combining readout at the quantum projection noise limit with strong dipolar interactions promises substantial gains in sensitivity. However, experimentally accessing this regime has remained a longstanding challenge. In this work, we demonstrate quantum-projection-noise-resolved readout of a strongly-interacting, two-dimensional ensemble of NV centers. Our approach leverages repetitive readout via the NV's intrinsic $^{15}$N nuclear memory at a moderate magnetic field ($\sim 0.3$ T), improving the readout fidelities by nearly an order of magnitude. This enables us to directly resolve the quantum projection noise of a coherent spin state and to watch the ensemble's intrinsic dipolar interactions shear this noise into an anisotropic profile. Our results open the door to direct measurements of spin squeezing and entanglement-enhanced sensing in the solid state.

AI.tldr: Repetitive readout via the NV's intrinsic 15N nuclear memory at ~0.3 T boosts readout fidelity by ~10x, enabling direct resolution of quantum projection noise in a strongly-interacting 2D NV ensemble and observation of dipolar-interaction-induced anisotropic noise shearing.
AI.motivation: The NV center is a leading quantum-sensing platform. Combining quantum-projection-noise-limited readout with strong dipolar interactions could substantially improve sensitivity, but reaching this regime experimentally has been a longstanding challenge.
AI.method: Repetitive readout exploiting the NV's intrinsic 15N nuclear memory at a moderate magnetic field (~0.3 T), applied to a strongly-interacting two-dimensional ensemble of NV centers to improve readout fidelities by nearly an order of magnitude.
AI.result: Achieved quantum-projection-noise-resolved readout, directly resolving the quantum projection noise of a coherent spin state and observing intrinsic dipolar interactions shear this noise into an anisotropic profile.
AI.conclusion: The results open the door to direct measurements of spin squeezing and entanglement-enhanced sensing in the solid state.

title: Large-scale quantum simulations of dissipative spin-1/2 Heisenberg chains
summary: A quantum many-body system coupled to an environment relaxes to a nonequilibrium steady state that can sustain order with no equilibrium counterpart. Computing such steady states is harder than closed-system dynamics as the density matrix problem squares the Hilbert-space dimension, and no free energy selects the steady state. The dissipative spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain is a benchmark example for nonequilibrium steady state physics; various methods have each calculated its phase diagram but do not agree, and a controlled determination at large system size has remained out of reach. Here we simulate the Lindblad dynamics of chains of up to 50 sites on the superconducting processor ibm_kingston -- 100 simultaneously active qubits at up to 1700 entangling-gate depths -- realizing the dissipation via Stinespring dilation. The system's dissipative evolution is a self-correcting mechanism that effectively erases errors, so hardware noise enters only as a weak competing dissipator. We measure static structure factors and resolve ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, spin-density-wave, and paramagnetic steady states, mapping the phase diagram with 117 quantum hardware data points across the $J_x$--$J_y$ plane. We uncover a rich non-equilibrium phase diagram of ordered phases with only remnants of the mean-field order, and where sharp transitions give way to the crossovers expected in one dimension. We also find the existence of an incipient (Trotter-induced) spin density wave phase, highlighting the potential of controlled Trotterization as a tool to engineer various magnetic phases in dissipative spin systems. Our quantum simulations largely settle the lingering uncertainty regarding the correct phase diagram of this benchmark system. Moreover, they show that quantum computers are now a feasible tool for addressing scientific questions involving dissipative quantum systems.

AI.motivation: Nonequilibrium steady states of dissipative quantum many-body systems can host order with no equilibrium analogue, but computing them is hard because the density-matrix problem squares the Hilbert-space dimension and no free energy selects the steady state. The dissipative spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain is a benchmark, yet prior methods disagree on its phase diagram and a controlled large-size determination has been out of reach.

The dissipative evolution acts as a self-correcting mechanism erasing errors, so hardware noise enters only as a weak competing dissipator. title: Adaptive detection of Rabi signals under composite hypotheses
summary: Motivated by searches for weak coherent drives, we formulate repeated quantum sensing with a fixed shot budget as an asymmetric composite hypothesis test. Taking Rabi sensing as a concrete example, we benchmark detection power, sensitivity, and Type-II error exponents in the resonant case with unknown signal amplitude and phase. We compare non-adaptive population and transverse readouts with a myopic Bayesian policy that selects each projective axis by maximizing the expected information gain in one step. The common decision statistic is a log Bayes factor, with a policy specific threshold calibrated under the null to enforce a common Type-I error. A weak signal expansion shows that population readout is phase independent but quadratic in amplitude, giving $n^{-1/4}$ sensitivity, whereas transverse readout is linear in amplitude and permits $n^{-1/2}$ sensitivity without adaptation, but is phase-dependent. In Monte Carlo pseudoexperiments, the adaptive policy exploits posterior information about the unknown direction to guide subsequent readouts; its sensitivity is consistent with $n^{-1/2}$ over the simulated large $n$ range and, at the largest simulated shot counts, outperforms the fixed transverse schedules. Its phase-averaged effective Type-II exponent also exceeds the non-adaptive references over the simulated range. These results demonstrate the finite budget value of exploiting nuisance parameter information under calibrated false positive control.

AI.motivation: Searches for weak coherent drives motivate formulating repeated quantum sensing with a fixed shot budget as an asymmetric composite hypothesis test, so that detection performance can be quantified under controlled false-positive rates when both signal amplitude and phase are unknown.
AI.method: Using Rabi sensing as a concrete example, the resonant case with unknown signal amplitude and phase is analyzed. Non-adaptive population and transverse readouts are compared with a myopic Bayesian policy that selects each projective axis by maximizing one-step expected information gain. The common decision statistic is a log Bayes factor, with a policy-specific threshold calibrated under the null to enforce a common Type-I error. title: Nonlocal Magic across the Many-Body Localization Crossover
summary: Nonlocal magic quantifies the minimum nonstabilizerness attainable under independent local unitary transformations on the two subsystems. Here, we use min-relative nonlocal magic (NLM) to characterize the crossover from ergodicity to many-body localization (MBL) in the random-field XXZ chain. Unlike entanglement entropy, NLM probes how entanglement is organized through the distance of the Schmidt spectrum from dyadic-flat stabilizer spectra. From weak to intermediate disorder, NLM evolves from an $O(1)$ Haar-like value into a size-enhanced dome, while entanglement remains volume-law, revealing a spectral reorganization not visible in the entropy. Deep in the MBL regime, a two-level cut-hybridization model captures the nearly binary Schmidt spectrum and explains why the mean and median NLM decay approximately as $W^{-1}$ and $W^{-2}$, respectively. Following a product-state quench, NLM overshoots and relaxes in the ergodic regime, whereas at strong disorder it grows slowly and approximately logarithmically. These results show that NLM resolves Schmidt-spectrum structure not visible in the entanglement entropy and provides a complementary probe of ergodicity breaking.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces min-relative nonlocal magic (NLM) as a probe of the ergodicity-to-MBL crossover in the random-field XXZ chain, showing it reveals Schmidt-spectrum reorganization invisible to entanglement entropy.
AI.motivation: Entanglement entropy is a standard probe of the ergodic-to-MBL transition but measures only the amount, not the organization, of entanglement. The authors seek a quantity that captures spectral structure of the Schmidt spectrum, motivating the use of nonlocal magic as a complementary diagnostic.
AI.method: They compute the min-relative nonlocal magic, defined as the minimum nonstabilizerness under independent local unitaries on the two subsystems, which measures the distance of the Schmidt spectrum from dyadic-flat stabilizer spectra. They study the random-field XXZ chain across disorder strengths and quench dynamics, and analyze the deep-MBL regime with a two-level cut-hybridization model.
AI.result: From weak to intermediate disorder, NLM evolves from an O(1) Haar-like value into a size-enhanced dome while entanglement remains volume-law. Deep in the MBL regime, the two-level cut-hybridization model yields a nearly binary Schmidt spectrum and explains mean and median NLM decays approximately as W^-1 and W^-2. After a product-state quench, NLM overshoots and relaxes in the ergodic regime but grows slowly and approximately logarithmically at strong disorder.
AI.conclusion: NLM resolves Schmidt-spectrum structure not visible in entanglement entropy and provides a complementary probe of ergodicity breaking.

title: The Transient Counting Statistics of Autonomous Quantum Clocks
summary: At the heart of every atomic clock is a quantum coherent emitter, the laser, that could in principle be treated autonomously. While their frequency or phase stability is typically studied in the semiclassical regime of a large number of emitted quanta, recent works on autonomous quantum clocks suggest that the few-quanta regime can offer statistical information in the temporal domain. This provides complementary means to probe the fundamental limits to precise timekeeping in the quantum regime. Motivated by these works, we consider simple models for two- and three-level quantum emitters subject to an athermal fueling through dephasing, which generically results in coherences in the steady state. A large deviation principle with finite-time contributions is used to identify the transient counting statistics and their dependence on the initial conditions. We conclude by discussing the implications for precise timekeeping and quantum sensing using autonomous quantum emitters as clocks in their transient regime.

AI.tldr: This work studies simple two- and three-level quantum emitters driven by athermal dephasing to analyze transient counting statistics and their implications for precision timekeeping and quantum sensing in autonomous quantum clocks.
AI.motivation: Atomic clocks rely on quantum coherent emitters (lasers), typically analyzed semiclassically with many emitted quanta. Recent autonomous quantum clock research suggests the few-quanta regime provides temporal-domain statistical information, offering complementary means to probe fundamental limits of quantum timekeeping. The authors are motivated to explore simple emitter models in this regime.
AI.method: The authors consider simple models of two- and three-level quantum emitters subject to athermal fueling via dephasing, which generically produces steady-state coherences. They apply a large deviation principle incorporating finite-time contributions to identify transient counting statistics and their dependence on initial conditions.
AI.result: The large deviation principle with finite-time contributions characterizes the transient counting statistics of the emitters and reveals how these statistics depend on the initial conditions. Athermal dephasing fueling yields steady-state coherences in these models.
AI.conclusion: The findings have implications for precise timekeeping and quantum sensing when autonomous quantum emitters are used as clocks in their transient regime, connecting few-quanta statistics to fundamental limits of quantum timekeeping.

title: Latent kinetic Ising models of neural spike trains
summary:
Inferring directed effective interactions from neuronal spike trains is a central inverse problem in statistical physics and computational neuroscience. Kinetic Ising models provide a tractable framework for this task, but their application to neural data typically requires binning spike trains into binary activity variables, discarding within-bin timing and conflating collective network dynamics with single-neuron history effects.
  We introduce SpiKIsing, a latent-variable model that separates these two levels of description. A discrete-time asymmetric kinetic Ising model describes collective network activity, while continuous-time, history-dependent point processes generate the observed spikes conditional on the latent states, accounting explicitly for refractoriness and post-spike recovery.
  We derive a variational mean-field expectation-maximization scheme in which the point-process likelihood enters as an effective observation field, enabling joint inference of latent activity, network couplings, and emission parameters. The framework extends naturally to maximum-a-posteriori inference with structured priors, including sparsity and a hierarchical extension favouring Dale-consistent outgoing interactions.
  We validate parameter recovery on matched synthetic data and test the method on spike trains generated by a recurrent conductance-based leaky integrate-and-fire network. In this setting, SpiKIsing recovers sparse connection structure and correctly classifies all excitatory and inhibitory neurons despite the substantial mismatch between the data-generating dynamics and the SpiKIsing model.

AI.tldr: SpiKIsing is a latent-variable model that couples an asymmetric kinetic Ising model of collective network activity with continuous-time point processes generating spikes, and is inferred via a variational mean-field EM scheme.
AI.motivation: Inferring directed effective interactions from spike trains is a central inverse problem, but standard kinetic Ising approaches require binning spikes into binary variables, which discards within-bin timing and conflates collective network dynamics with single-neuron history effects.
AI.method: The method separates two description levels: a discrete-time asymmetric kinetic Ising model for collective activity, and continuous-time history-dependent point processes for observed spikes conditional on latent states, explicitly modeling refractoriness and post-spike recovery. A variational mean-field expectation-maximization scheme treats the point-process likelihood as an effective observation field, enabling joint inference of latent activity, couplings, and emission parameters. It extends to MAP inference with structured priors, including sparsity and a hierarchical prior favoring Dale-consistent outgoing interactions.
AI.result: Parameter recovery is validated on matched synthetic data and tested on spike trains from a recurrent conductance-based leaky integrate-and-fire network. SpiKIsing recovers sparse connection structure and correctly classifies all excitatory and inhibitory neurons despite substantial mismatch between the data-generating dynamics and the model.
AI.conclusion: SpiKIsing provides a principled framework for joint inference of latent neural activity, effective network couplings, and emission parameters from spike trains, and remains robust under model mismatch, supporting its use for recovering directed interactions and cell-type identity.

title: Hyperbolic color codes with constant rate and polynomial distance
summary: Recent advances in quantum hardware relax the strict geometric-locality constraints traditionally imposed on quantum error-correcting codes, motivating interest in high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. At the same time, color codes provide a particularly rich setting for fault-tolerant quantum computation, underlying protocols such as single-shot error correction and self-correcting quantum computation. Hyperbolic color codes provide a class of high-rate qLDPC codes that also retain the structural features of color codes relevant to fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, previous constructions of hyperbolic color codes have achieved at most logarithmic code distance. In this work, we construct hyperbolic color codes with both constant rate and polynomial distance by building on arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds that support polynomial-distance hyperbolic toric codes. Our construction applies in arbitrary dimension \(D\geq 4\). In even dimensions, the resulting type-\(D/2\) color codes have constant encoding rate and polynomial distance, while in other cases the number of logical qubits and the code distance both exhibit polynomial scaling. We further derive explicit exponents for polynomial lower bounds as functions of the dimension and code type. These results establish a family of hyperbolic color codes simultaneously achieving constant rate and polynomial distance and providing a testbed to explore fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols that combine high-rate quantum codes with the structural advantages of color codes.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs hyperbolic color codes with constant rate and polynomial distance in arbitrary dimension D ≥ 4, based on arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds.
AI.motivation: Advances in quantum hardware relax strict geometric-locality constraints, motivating high-rate qLDPC codes. Color codes offer rich structure for fault-tolerant quantum computation, and hyperbolic color codes combine high rate with these structural features, but prior constructions achieved only logarithmic distance.
AI.method: The authors build on arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds that support polynomial-distance hyperbolic toric codes to construct hyperbolic color codes in arbitrary dimension D ≥ 4. In even dimensions these yield type-D/2 color codes; explicit polynomial lower-bound exponents are derived as functions of dimension and code type.
AI.result: In even dimensions, the type-D/2 color codes have constant encoding rate and polynomial distance. In other cases, both the number of logical qubits and the code distance exhibit polynomial scaling. Explicit exponents for the polynomial lower bounds are provided.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a family of hyperbolic color codes simultaneously achieving constant rate and polynomial distance, offering a testbed for fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols combining high-rate quantum codes with the structural advantages of color codes.

title: Bias-Induced Crossover in Absolute Capacity of Dense Associative Memory
summary: The absolute capacity of dense associative memory has mainly been analyzed for unbiased patterns. Here we examine the effect of bias in centered binary patterns under the Krotov-Hopfield single-site criterion $P_{\mathrm{error}}=1/N$, where $P_{\mathrm{error}}$ is the probability that a single-site flip lowers the energy of a stored pattern and $N$ is the number of neurons. Each pattern component takes $1-q$ with probability $q$ and $-q$ otherwise, where $0<q\le1/2$. For polynomial interactions of order $n$, a signal-to-noise analysis gives an absolute capacity of order $N^{n-1}/\ln N$ at $q=1/2$. For fixed $q<1/2$, however, the capacity is $O(N^{n/2})$ for even $n\ge4$ and $O(N^{(n+1)/2})$ for odd $n\ge5$. For $n=3$, both the unbiased and fixed-bias capacities remain $O(N^2/\ln N)$. For $n\ge4$, these different asymptotic forms imply a nonuniform large-$N$ limit near $q=1/2$. Asymptotic matching predicts a bias-induced crossover in the region $1-2q=O(\ln N/N^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor-1})$. The crossover originates from a bias-dependent crosstalk mean that reduces the stability of sites carrying the more frequent value $-q$. Computer simulations are compared with the finite-size conditioned-Gaussian predictions. An activity-dependent control potential that cancels the conditional crosstalk mean restores the $N^{n-1}/\ln N$ capacity for fixed $0<q<1/2$ within the conditioned-Gaussian approximation.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how bias in centered binary patterns reduces the absolute capacity of dense associative memory for polynomial interactions of order n, deriving distinct asymptotic capacity regimes depending on whether bias is zero, fixed, or vanishing in the large-N limit.
AI.motivation: Existing capacity analyses of dense associative memory assume unbiased patterns (q=1/2). Real stored patterns are often biased, so the authors extend the Krotov-Hopfield single-site analysis to characterize how nonzero bias q affects absolute capacity for general polynomial interaction order n.
AI.method: They use a signal-to-noise analysis under the Krotov-Hopfield error criterion P_error=1/N, with centered binary patterns taking value 1-q with probability q and -q otherwise. They derive asymptotic capacities for polynomial interactions of order n, perform asymptotic matching, compare with finite-size conditioned-Gaussian predictions, and add an activity-dependent control potential that cancels the conditional crosstalk mean.
AI.result: At q=1/2 the capacity is order N^{n-1}/ln N. For fixed q<1/2 it becomes O(N^{n/2}) for even n>=4 and O(N^{(n+1)/2}) for odd n>=5, while n=3 retains O(N^2/ln N) in both cases. These differing forms yield a nonuniform large-N limit near q=1/2, with asymptotic matching predicting a bias-induced crossover when 1-2q=O(ln N/N^{floor(n/2)-1}), caused by a bias-dependent crosstalk mean that destabilizes sites carrying the more frequent value -q. Simulations agree with finite-size conditioned-Gaussian predictions.
AI.conclusion: Bias strongly degrades absolute capacity for high-order interactions (n>=4), producing a crossover region where the capacity transitions between scaling laws. An activity-dependent control potential restores the N^{n-1}/ln N capacity even for fixed bias within the conditioned-Gaussian approximation.

title: Pulse-Level Compilation of Measurement-Free Recovery in Transmon Circuits
summary: Quantum error correction commonly relies on syndrome measurement, decoding, and conditional feedback. We numerically show that the conditional spectrum of an interacting transmon circuit can compile a local recovery rule into a fixed open-loop control cycle. In a four-bit repetition-code ring, the resulting input-independent control slows the decay of logical coherence under Pauli-\(X\) noise and stabilizes logical-one population under data relaxation relative to uncorrected references. Its local, bounded-degree architecture provides a hardware-native framework for extending compiled recovery control to larger quantum networks.

AI.tldr: A numerically demonstrated open-loop control cycle in an interacting transmon circuit compiles a local recovery rule, slowing logical decoherence and stabilizing logical states in a four-bit repetition-code ring.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum error correction requires syndrome measurement, decoding, and conditional feedback, which imposes overhead and complexity. The paper seeks a hardware-native alternative that avoids explicit measurement-based feedback by embedding recovery into the circuit's dynamics.
AI.method: Numerical study of the conditional spectrum of an interacting transmon circuit to compile a local recovery rule into a fixed, input-independent open-loop control cycle, applied to a four-bit repetition-code ring under Pauli-X noise and data relaxation.
AI.result: The input-independent control slows the decay of logical coherence under Pauli-X noise and stabilizes logical-one population under data relaxation, both relative to uncorrected references.
AI.conclusion: A local, bounded-degree architecture offers a hardware-native framework for extending compiled recovery control to larger quantum networks.

title: Coupling spherical p-spin systems
summary: Spherical p-spin models provide a mean-field framework for glassy dynamics. Coupling such systems opens a controlled way to probe how they evolve jointly, develop cross correlations, and possibly share common aging scales. We study spherical p-spin systems with site-independent inter-system couplings and generally correlated quenched disorders. We derive closed multi-subsystem two-time equations for correlations, responses, and spherical constraints. A marginal one-step replica-symmetry-breaking construction provides static benchmarks for overlap plateaux, aging crossover scales, and effective temperatures. We then specialize to two ferromagnetically coupled p=3 systems and compare dynamical data with marginal 1RSB predictions. Independent quenched disorders reduce the equal-time correlation between the systems below its disorder-free value, while correlated disorders enhance it. For sufficiently strong coupling, finite-time fluctuation-dissipation estimates within and between the systems are compatible with a common effective temperature even when one or both subsystems would equilibrate as a paramagnet in isolation. This common value lies above the effective temperatures that the constituent systems would have separately and increases with disorder correlation and coupling strength. The marginal 1RSB value T/m captures these trends but is slightly below the finite-time dynamical estimate. For weak coupling, the dynamical results instead suggest that two aging regimes develop for each system, with partial equilibration within each. We perform a marginal replica analysis with two-step breaking, whose predictions compare favorably with the numerical measurements. Our numerical accuracy is insufficient to determine whether the observed finite-time crossover will eventually become a sharp transition.

AI.tldr: This paper studies coupled spherical p-spin models to understand joint glassy dynamics, deriving multi-subsystem two-time equations and comparing marginal 1RSB (and 2RSB for weak coupling) predictions with numerical simulations of two coupled p=3 systems.
AI.motivation: Spherical p-spin models offer a mean-field framework for glassy dynamics, and coupling such systems provides a controlled way to probe how they evolve jointly, develop cross correlations, and possibly share common aging scales.
AI.method: The authors consider spherical p-spin systems with site-independent inter-system couplings and generally correlated quenched disorders. They derive closed multi-subsystem two-time equations for correlations, responses, and spherical constraints, and use a marginal one-step replica-symmetry-breaking (1RSB) construction as a static benchmark. They specialize to two ferromagnetically coupled p=3 systems, comparing dynamical data with marginal 1RSB predictions, and perform a marginal replica analysis with two-step breaking for weak coupling.
AI.result: Independent quenched disorders reduce the equal-time inter-system correlation below its disorder-free value, while correlated disorders enhance it. For strong coupling, finite-time fluctuation-dissipation estimates within and between systems are compatible with a common effective temperature, even when a subsystem would equilibrate as a paramagnet in isolation; this common value exceeds the separate effective temperatures and rises with disorder correlation and coupling strength, with the marginal 1RSB value T/m capturing the trends but lying slightly below the dynamical estimate. For weak coupling, two aging regimes develop per system with partial equilibration, and a marginal two-step breaking replica analysis matches the measurements well.
AI.conclusion: Coupled spherical p-spin systems exhibit a shared effective temperature under strong coupling and multiple aging regimes under weak coupling. The marginal 1RSB (and 2RSB) predictions qualitatively and semi-quantitatively match the dynamical results, though numerical accuracy is insufficient to determine whether the observed finite-time crossover becomes a sharp transition.

title: Designs without disorder: unitary $k$-designs from a single-site bulk defect
summary: We show that an $O(1)$ local defect is sufficient to generate approximate unitary $k$-designs from an otherwise integrable quantum many-body system. Using a two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol with temporal sampling, we demonstrate this mechanism in a fixed-magnetization sector of deterministic XXZ spin chains with a single integrability-breaking bulk defect. We derive an analytical selection rule for the Pauli kicks and show that symmetry-preserving strings with a specific domain-wall count, fixed by the couplings, govern design formation. An exhaustive search over all admissible Pauli strings identifies a broad family of kicks that produce designs in the chaotic regime, whereas no such kicks exist in the integrable limit, including for boundary defects. We further show that the design-forming mechanism remains effective for weak bulk defects as the system size increases.

AI.tldr: An O(1) local defect suffices to generate approximate unitary k-designs from an otherwise integrable XXZ spin chain, via a temporally-sampled two-Pauli-kick protocol.
AI.motivation: Understand the minimal resources needed to turn an integrable many-body system into one capable of complex (design-forming) dynamics, i.e., whether a single O(1) integrability-breaking perturbation can generate approximate unitary k-designs.
AI.method: Two-Pauli-kick (2PK) protocol with temporal sampling applied to a fixed-magnetization sector of deterministic XXZ chains containing a single integrability-breaking bulk defect. Analytical derivation of a selection rule for the Pauli kicks, plus exhaustive search over all admissible Pauli strings in both chaotic and integrable limits, including boundary-defect comparisons.
AI.result: A broad family of kicks produces designs in the chaotic regime; no such kicks exist in the integrable limit (including boundary defects). Symmetry-preserving strings with a specific domain-wall count, fixed by the couplings, govern design formation, and the mechanism persists for weak bulk defects at increasing system size.
AI.conclusion: A single O(1) local defect is sufficient to generate approximate unitary k-designs from an otherwise integrable system, with the design-forming mechanism remaining effective for weak bulk defects as system size grows.

title: Investigating Interacting Fermionic Models with Locality-Preserving Qubit Encodings
summary: We investigate the utility of the locality-preserving Derby-Klassen (DK) fermion-to-qubit mapping [arXiv:2003.06939] for variational quantum simulation of two-dimensional $t$-$V$ and Fermi-Hubbard models. The DK mapping preserves the locality of fermionic interactions with an enlarged Hilbert space, thereby requiring additional constraints that define the physical sector. We incorporate these constraints directly into a Hamiltonian Variational Ansätz (HVA) through Clifford-gate state preparation and use the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) to show that the low-energy properties of the resulting qubit Hamiltonian are accurately reproduced. We further exploit particle-number conservation inherent in the ansätz to resolve distinct symmetry sectors and reliably access degenerate states. Consequently, we benchmark the DK-HVA against Jordan-Wigner-based variational circuits at nonzero chemical potential, where particle-hole symmetry and the associated half-filled sign-free condition are absent. Finally, we demonstrate the advantage of locality-preserving mappings in higher-dimensional fermionic systems, where the conventional Jordan-Wigner (JW) transformation generates increasingly long Pauli strings and corresponding circuit overheads. We further extend the framework to the spinful Fermi-Hubbard model and identify a tradeoff between fermionic-mode placement and the locality of hopping and on-site interaction terms. These results establish a practical framework combining locality-preserving fermion-to-qubit mappings, constraint-preserving Clifford state preparation, and symmetry-preserving variational circuits, that trades auxiliary-qubit and stabilizer-preparation overhead for reduced operator nonlocality, providing a practical route toward resource-efficient quantum simulation of higher-dimensional interacting fermionic systems.

AI.tldr: This work benchmarks the locality-preserving Derby-Klassen (DK) fermion-to-qubit mapping against Jordan-Wigner for variational quantum simulation of 2D t-V and Fermi-Hubbard models, embedding the mapping's physical-sector constraints into an HVA via Clifford state preparation and exploiting particle-number conservation to resolve symmetry sectors.
AI.motivation: In higher-dimensional fermionic systems, the conventional Jordan-Wigner transformation produces increasingly long Pauli strings, causing severe circuit overhead. Locality-preserving mappings like DK reduce operator nonlocality but enlarge the Hilbert space and require additional constraints to define the physical sector, so their practical utility for variational simulation needs systematic assessment.
AI.method: The authors incorporate DK's physical-sector constraints directly into a Hamiltonian Variational Ansatz through Clifford-gate state preparation, then apply VQE to reproduce low-energy properties of the resulting qubit Hamiltonian. Particle-number conservation in the ansatz is exploited to resolve distinct symmetry sectors and access degenerate states. DK-HVA is benchmarked against JW-based variational circuits at nonzero chemical potential, where particle-hole symmetry and the half-filled sign-free condition are absent, and extended to the spinful Fermi-Hubbard model.
AI.result: VQE with the constraint-preserving DK-HVA accurately reproduces low-energy properties, and particle-number conservation reliably resolves symmetry sectors and degenerate states. DK-HVA outperforms JW-based circuits at nonzero chemical potential. In higher dimensions, DK avoids the growing Pauli-string length and circuit overhead of JW. For the spinful Fermi-Hubbard model, a tradeoff emerges between fermionic-mode placement and the locality of hopping versus on-site interaction terms.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a practical framework combining locality-preserving fermion-to-qubit mappings, constraint-preserving Clifford state preparation, and symmetry-preserving variational circuits. It trades auxiliary-qubit and stabilizer-preparation overhead for reduced operator nonlocality, offering a resource-efficient route to quantum simulation of higher-dimensional interacting fermionic systems.

title: Noise-induced classical phases in optimally-unraveled random quantum circuits
summary: We study the classical simulability of open quantum dynamics using random Clifford circuits doped with non-Clifford phase rotations and subject to local noise. We unravel the dynamics into stochastic quantum trajectories simulated with Clifford-augmented matrix product states, and introduce a simulation cost that quantifies the classical resources required. Optimizing this cost over stochastic unravelings, we identify noise-induced classical phases: extended parameter regions in which the dynamics can be fully disentangled by Clifford operations at arbitrary circuit depth. Their existence depends on both the noise model \emph{and} the unraveling. Using a geometric representation of quantum channels, we analytically determine optimal unravelings for a broad class of noise models, with numerical simulations confirming the predicted phase boundaries. We further relate the optimal cost to the unraveling-independent nonstabilizerness of the channel and show that, together with trajectory-resolved entanglement and nonstabilizerness, it classifies distinct dynamical regimes. Finally, we show that these classical phases disappear in the averaged density-matrix description, where no unraveling freedom remains. Our results show that the emergence of classicality in noisy random circuits depends on the measurement scheme adopted to probe it, and paves the way to further studies on the classical simulability of driven-dissipative dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates when noisy random Clifford circuits doped with non-Clifford rotations become classically simulable, showing that noise can induce "classical phases" whose existence depends on both the noise model and the stochastic unraveling used to simulate the dynamics.
AI.motivation: Understanding the classical simulability of open quantum dynamics is a central question, and it is unclear how local noise interacts with non-Clifford resources to enable or hinder efficient classical simulation. The authors aim to identify whether noise can genuinely restore classicality and how this depends on the probing/measurement scheme.
AI.method: The dynamics are unraveled into stochastic quantum trajectories simulated with Clifford-augmented matrix product states. A simulation cost quantifying required classical resources is introduced and optimized over stochastic unravelings. Using a geometric representation of quantum channels, optimal unravelings are analytically determined for a broad class of noise models, with numerical simulations confirming predicted phase boundaries. The optimal cost is related to the unraveling-independent nonstabilizerness of the channel.
AI.result: Noise-induced classical phases are identified as extended parameter regions where dynamics can be fully disentangled by Clifford operations at arbitrary circuit depth. Their existence depends on both the noise model and the unraveling. The optimal cost, together with trajectory-resolved entanglement and nonstabilizerness, classifies distinct dynamical regimes. These classical phases disappear in the averaged density-matrix description, where no unraveling freedom remains.
AI.conclusion: The emergence of classicality in noisy random circuits depends on the measurement scheme adopted to probe it, paving the way for further studies on the classical simulability of driven-dissipative dynamics.

title: Towards Block-Level Fault-Tolerant Quantum Simulation on Small High-Rate Non-CSS Codes
summary: Small high-rate non-CSS stabilizer codes provide compact platforms for encoded quantum computation, but mixed-Pauli checks and limited native transversal logical gates complicate fault-tolerant dynamics. Block-level constructions offer an alternative by mapping an entire logical block to a physical circuit rather than compiling separately protected logical gates. We investigate this approach using the high-rate [[8,3,3]] non-CSS code and logical Trotter circuits as a testbed. We construct flagged syndrome-extraction circuits and establish a circuit-level memory pseudo-threshold near \(1.5\times10^{-3}\). We then apply our symplectic-transvection construction, which maps a logical Trotter circuit to a physical circuit with the same block pattern for any stabilizer code. Although this mapping preserves the intended unitary algebraically, encoded Trotter circuits exhibit asymmetry between logical-\(X\) and logical-\(Z\) failure channels. Single-fault analysis identifies the mechanism: a fault on the shared parity ancilla can propagate through the uncomputation network into an undetectable logical operator, reducing the effective circuit distance in the affected sector. We evaluate flag-conditioned recovery, biased-noise decoding, CliNR resource verification, flag postselection, and asymmetric gate-noise models. These methods suppress propagated faults but do not simultaneously suppress both logical sectors in the realistic configurations studied. A diagnostic protected limit removing the identified malignant first-order locations restores pseudo-threshold behavior in both sectors, approaching memory performance. These results demonstrate the potential of block-level logical constructions for non-CSS codes without rich native transversal gate sets and the joint protection of the parity network, analog rotation, and recovery required to preserve fault-tolerant distance.

AI.tldr: The paper studies block-level fault-tolerant quantum computation using a high-rate [[8,3,3]] non-CSS stabilizer code. It constructs flagged syndrome-extraction circuits, establishes a circuit-level memory pseudo-threshold (~1.5×10⁻³), and applies a symplectic-transvection mapping of logical Trotter circuits to physical circuits. The key finding is an asymmetry between logical-X and logical-Z failure channels caused by faults on a shared parity ancilla propagating into undetectable logical operators.
AI.motivation: Small high-rate non-CSS stabilizer codes are attractive for compact encoded computation, but mixed-Pauli checks and limited native transversal logical gates make fault-tolerant dynamics difficult. Block-level constructions, which map an entire logical block to a physical circuit instead of compiling separately protected logical gates, offer a promising alternative that has not been thoroughly investigated for non-CSS codes lacking rich native transversal gate sets.
AI.method: The authors use the [[8,3,3]] non-CSS code and logical Trotter circuits as a testbed. They (1) construct flagged syndrome-extraction circuits and measure the circuit-level memory pseudo-threshold; (2) apply a symplectic-transvection construction that maps a logical Trotter circuit to a physical circuit with the same block pattern for any stabilizer code; (3) perform single-fault analysis to identify the failure mechanism; and (4) evaluate flag-conditioned recovery, biased-noise decoding, CliNR resource verification, flag postselection, and asymmetric gate-noise models, plus a diagnostic protected limit.
AI.result: The circuit-level memory pseudo-threshold is near 1.5×10⁻³. Although the symplectic-transvection mapping preserves the intended unitary algebraically, encoded Trotter circuits show asymmetry between logical-X and logical-Z failure channels. Single-fault analysis reveals that a fault on the shared parity ancilla propagates through the uncomputation network into an undetectable logical operator, reducing the effective circuit distance in the affected sector. The mitigation methods suppress propagated faults but do not simultaneously suppress both logical sectors in realistic configurations. A diagnostic protected limit removing the malignant first-order locations restores pseudo-threshold behavior in both sectors, approaching memory performance.
AI.conclusion: Block-level logical constructions are viable for non-CSS codes without rich native transversal gate sets. However, preserving fault-tolerant distance requires joint protection of the parity network, analog rotation, and recovery, since these components interact to create asymmetric and potentially undetectable logical failures.

title: Why Are We Unrolling? The Importance of Structured Quantum Programs for Compilation
summary: As quantum software stacks scale up to support future fault-tolerant quantum hardware and algorithms, quantum compilation is becoming an increasingly important component of the stack. How do we ensure that our software stacks support dynamic algorithms, including patterns such as mid-circuit measurement feedforward and repeat-until-success, with hundreds of logical qubits and billions of quantum operations? To do so, we must re-think how we represent quantum programs beyond straight-line circuits, to representations that include classical structure and dynamism, and make this the default representation to consider when performing quantum compilation. In this work, we present important patterns and algorithms from fault-tolerant quantum applications which admit a structured representation that we argue is crucial to preserve, and set a challenge to the community to compile such representations without unrolling them into straight-line quantum circuits. We also explore the status quo of structured program support in quantum software, and ask ourselves the rhetorical question: how much more efficient can we make quantum compilation tooling when we take into account the additional information from classical structure?

AI.tldr: Quantum compilation must evolve beyond straight-line circuits to natively support structured, dynamic quantum programs with classical control, and this paper presents motivating patterns, algorithms, and a community challenge to compile such representations without unrolling.
AI.motivation: As quantum software stacks scale to support fault-tolerant hardware and algorithms, quantum compilation becomes a critical component. Ensuring stacks support dynamic algorithms (e.g., mid-circuit measurement feedforward, repeat-until-success) at scales of hundreds of logical qubits and billions of quantum operations requires rethinking program representation beyond straight-line circuits to include classical structure and dynamism.
AI.method: The paper surveys important patterns and algorithms from fault-tolerant quantum applications that admit a structured representation argued to be crucial to preserve. It proposes making structured (classical-plus-quantum) representations the default for quantum compilation, sets a challenge to compile such representations without unrolling into straight-line circuits, and examines the status quo of structured program support in existing quantum software.
AI.result: The work identifies structured patterns and algorithms from fault-tolerant applications that benefit from representation-level preservation, and assesses the current (limited) support for structured programs in quantum software tooling.
AI.conclusion: Structured program representations, rather than straight-line circuits, should be the default for quantum compilation. Leveraging classical structure offers significant potential efficiency gains, though realizing this requires community effort to compile structured representations directly.

title: Utility-Based Path Selection and Configuration in Quantum Networks via Layered Shortest Paths
summary: A path in a quantum network is a chain of repeaters that distributes entanglement between two users. Selecting a path requires balancing the rate and quality (e.g., fidelity) of the delivered entanglement, but these quantities, unlike standard routing metrics, compose non-additively. The problem is compounded by link-level configuration choices (e.g., distillation rounds or emitter brightness tuning), each trading rate against fidelity, so that a path's performance depends jointly on its route and its per-link settings. We cast this joint path selection and configuration problem as a shortest path computation on a layered graph whose layers track discretized end-to-end fidelity. A single run returns the full rate fidelity Pareto frontier, from which the path maximizing any nondecreasing utility function of rate and fidelity can be selected. We prove that for certain utility functions (including the secret key rate of BB84), the method is a fully polynomial time approximation scheme, returning a near-optimal path within a specified tolerance. We further characterize exactly when cheaper scalarization-based routing suffices: it is optimal for utility functions with convex fidelity profiles, but can be arbitrarily suboptimal otherwise (e.g., for step-like, sigmoidal utilities), whereas the layered method remains reliable in all cases.

AI.tldr: This paper frames joint path selection and per-link configuration in quantum networks as a shortest-path problem on a layered graph indexed by discretized end-to-end fidelity, yielding the full rate-fidelity Pareto frontier in one run.
AI.motivation: Routing in quantum networks differs from classical routing because rate and fidelity compose non-additively along a repeater chain. Link-level configuration choices (distillation rounds, emitter brightness) further trade rate against fidelity, so path performance depends jointly on route and per-link settings. Standard scalarization-based routing may fail under such non-additive, non-convex trade-offs, motivating a method that handles the joint problem reliably.
AI.method: The joint path selection and configuration problem is cast as a shortest-path computation on a layered graph whose layers track discretized end-to-end fidelity. A single run returns the complete rate-fidelity Pareto frontier, from which the path maximizing any nondecreasing utility of rate and fidelity can be chosen. The authors prove that for certain utilities, including the BB84 secret key rate, the method is a fully polynomial time approximation scheme (FPTAS) returning a near-optimal path within a specified tolerance, and they characterize exactly when cheaper scalarization-based routing suffices.
AI.result: The layered method returns the full rate-fidelity Pareto frontier in one run and yields an FPTAS for utilities such as the BB84 secret key rate. Scalarization-based routing is shown to be optimal for utility functions with convex fidelity profiles but can be arbitrarily suboptimal otherwise, e.g., for step-like or sigmoidal utilities, where the layered method remains reliable.
AI.conclusion: Layered-graph shortest path provides a principled, reliably near-optimal solution to joint quantum-network path selection and link configuration, whereas scalarization-based routing is only safe under convex fidelity profiles and can fail badly for non-convex utilities.

title: Coupling Structure Determines Communication Regimes in Discrete Quantum Convolutional Channels
summary:
We study the recently developed theory of quantum convolution for discrete-variable quantum systems. We classify the discrete quantum convolutional channels generated by an invertible $2\times2$ coupling matrix and a fixed environmental state according to which entries of the coupling ma- trix vanish. Under role-preserving basis relabelings, matrices with all four entries nonzero form $d-2$ canonical cross-ratio classes, whereas matrices with exactly one vanishing entry split into four inequivalent branches. We determine the optimized one-shot Holevo information and the classical, quantum, and private capacities for all four one-entry-vanishing branches. If a diago- nal entry vanishes, the channel is an entanglement-breaking measure-and-prepare orbit channel: its classical capacity equals a relative entropy coherence of the environmental state, whereas its quantum and private capacities vanish. If an off-diagonal entry vanishes, the channel is a degradable generalized-dephasing channel: one complete orthonormal basis is transmitted without error, whereas the quantum and private capacities are determined by the entropy deficit of the environ-ental state
  after dephasing in the conjugate basis. Thus, the position of a single vanishing entry selects two qualitatively different communication regimes. When all four entries are nonzero, the channels are irreducibly Weyl covariant, reducing the classical-capacity problem to a regularized minimum-output-entropy problem. For the unique fully nonzero coupling class in the single-qutrit case, we further derive an exact Holevo formula for a depolarized one-parameter family and identify its entanglement-breaking threshold.

AI.tldr: Quantum convolutional channels from an invertible 2x2 coupling matrix and fixed environment are classified by vanishing entries: one vanishing entry yields two distinct regimes (entanglement-breaking measure-and-prepare if diagonal, degradable generalized dephasing if off-diagonal), while fully nonzero couplings are irreducibly Weyl covariant. Capacities are computed for each branch, plus an exact Holevo formula for the single-qutrit fully nonzero class.
AI.motivation: Quantum convolution is a recently developed framework for discrete-variable quantum systems, but the structure and communication capabilities of the resulting channels were not systematically understood. This work aims to classify these channels and determine their capacities.
AI.method: The channels are generated by an invertible 2x2 coupling matrix and a fixed environmental state. They are classified by which entries of the coupling matrix vanish, up to role-preserving basis relabelings: fully nonzero matrices form d-2 canonical cross-ratio classes, exactly-one-vanishing matrices split into four inequivalent branches. For the one-entry-vanishing branches the optimized one-shot Holevo information and classical, quantum, and private capacities are computed. For the fully nonzero case, Weyl covariance is identified, and an exact Holevo formula is derived for a depolarized one-parameter family in the single-qutrit case.
AI.result: If a diagonal entry vanishes, the channel is entanglement-breaking (measure-and-prepare orbit channel): classical capacity equals a relative entropy coherence of the environmental state, and quantum and private capacities vanish. If an off-diagonal entry vanishes, the channel is a degradable generalized-dephasing channel: one complete orthonormal basis is transmitted without error, and quantum and private capacities are set by the entropy deficit of the environment after dephasing in the conjugate basis. Fully nonzero couplings are irreducibly Weyl covariant, reducing classical capacity to a regularized minimum-output-entropy problem. For the unique fully nonzero single-qutrit class, an exact Holevo formula and the entanglement-breaking threshold are identified.
AI.conclusion: The position of a single vanishing entry in the coupling matrix selects two qualitatively different communication regimes, and the fully nonzero case connects classical capacity to a regularized minimum-output-entropy problem. The classification thus organizes discrete quantum convolutional channels by their information-theoretic behavior.

title: Link-middle-cut lower bounds for Clifford circuit synthesis
summary: Minimizing the number of CNOT gates required to synthesize a Clifford operator is a central problem in quantum circuit optimization. We extend the link--middle--cut (LMC) framework for linear reversible circuits to Clifford operators represented by binary symplectic tableaux. By introducing block-support connectivity graphs and determinantal invariants, we obtain efficiently computable lower bounds on ancilla-free CNOT complexity. We prove that these bounds are tight for qubit permutations: a permutation of $n$ qubits with $k$ cycles requires exactly $3(n-k)$ CNOT gates, even when arbitrary one-qubit Clifford gates are available. We also derive efficiently computable bounds for synthesis up to a permutation of the output qubits, corresponding to free qubit relabeling. Finally, we further demonstrate the utility of the bound by using it as an admissible heuristic for $A^*$-based Clifford synthesis and show that, on benchmark instances, the resulting search can prove optimality beyond what was possible with earlier SAT-based methods, and that it may be used in combination with earlier $A^*$ heuristics to improve the CNOT counts obtained through heuristic search.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the LMC framework to ancilla-free CNOT complexity of Clifford operators via binary symplectic tableaux, introduces block-support connectivity graphs and determinantal invariants to derive efficiently computable lower bounds, proves tightness for qubit permutations at 3(n-k) CNOTs, and uses the bound as an A* heuristic for optimal Clifford synthesis beyond prior SAT methods.
AI.motivation: Minimizing CNOT gates for synthesizing a Clifford operator is central to quantum circuit optimization. Existing frameworks such as link--middle--cut (LMC) were designed for linear reversible circuits, leaving a gap for general Clifford operators and for efficient, provably tight lower bounds on ancilla-free CNOT complexity.
AI.method: The authors generalize the LMC framework from linear reversible circuits to Clifford operators represented by binary symplectic tableaux. They introduce block-support connectivity graphs and determinantal invariants to compute lower bounds on ancilla-free CNOT complexity, derive bounds for synthesis up to output-qubit permutation (free relabeling), and employ the bound as an admissible heuristic in A*-based Clifford synthesis.
AI.result: The derived bounds are proven tight for qubit permutations: a permutation of n qubits with k cycles requires exactly 3(n-k) CNOT gates even with arbitrary one-qubit Clifford gates. On benchmark instances, A* search using the bound proves optimality beyond earlier SAT-based methods and, combined with prior A* heuristics, improves CNOT counts obtained by heuristic search.
AI.conclusion: The extended LMC framework yields efficiently computable, tight lower bounds for ancilla-free Clifford CNOT complexity, validates the permutation case exactly, and provides an effective admissible heuristic that advances both optimal and heuristic Clifford synthesis on benchmarks.

title: $d$-pod realization of nonadiabatic holonomic quantum computation
summary: Holonomic quantum computation (HQC) realizes quantum gates through non-Abelian geometric phases, providing an experimentally accessible approach to quantum control. While the nonadiabatic HQC framework has been extensively developed for three-level $Λ$ systems encoding qubits, its systematic extension to higher-dimensional qudits remains largely unexplored. In this work, we generalize nonadiabatic HQC to a $d$-pod configuration, where a single excited state is coupled to $d$ ground states, the latter forming the computational subspace. This scheme enables universal holonomic single- and two-qudit gates using only optical or microwave pulses on trapped atoms or ions, offering an efficient route to implement a discrete universal gate set with minimal pulse coordination. As an explicit example, we analyze in detail the qutrit ($d=3$) case, demonstrating compact realizations of single- and two-qutrit holonomic gates, each gate requiring at most two loops in the Grassmannian generated by at most three pulses.

AI.tldr: This work generalizes nonadiabatic holonomic quantum computation from three-level Λ systems to a d-pod configuration, enabling universal holonomic single- and two-qudit gates with minimal pulse coordination, with the qutrit case analyzed in detail.
AI.motivation: Nonadiabatic HQC has been well developed for three-level Λ systems encoding qubits, but its systematic extension to higher-dimensional qudits remains largely unexplored. There is a need for a general framework that scales HQC to qudits.
AI.method: The authors generalize nonadiabatic HQC to a d-pod configuration, where a single excited state couples to d ground states forming the computational subspace. Gates are implemented using only optical or microwave pulses on trapped atoms or ions.
AI.result: The scheme enables universal holonomic single- and two-qudit gates with minimal pulse coordination. The qutrit (d=3) case is analyzed in detail, showing compact realizations of single- and two-qutrit holonomic gates, each requiring at most two loops in the Grassmannian generated by at most three pulses.
AI.conclusion: The d-pod generalization provides an efficient route to a discrete universal gate set for qudits, extending HQC beyond qubits with experimentally feasible pulse sequences.

title: Error-corrected function estimation advantage in multiparameter Hamiltonians
summary: We establish the ultimate precision limits for estimating a function of multiple Hamiltonian parameters in the presence of Markovian noise. By reducing multiparameter function estimation to an optimization over effective single-parameter embeddings, we derive tight bounds on the quantum Fisher information. We identify a necessary and sufficient functional Hamiltonian-not-in-Lindblad-span condition for Heisenberg-limited scaling in time. When this condition holds, we construct a code that simultaneously removes the noise and nuisance Hamiltonian parameters while preserving the target signal. When it fails, we derive the optimal standard quantum-limit coefficient and show that it is asymptotically attainable using approximate quantum error correction. Finally, we demonstrate that direct function estimation can substantially outperform estimating all parameters individually and subsequently evaluating the function. This advantage can scale with both the evolution time and the number of parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper derives ultimate precision limits for estimating a function of multiple Hamiltonian parameters under Markovian noise, establishing a sharp Hamiltonian-not-in-Lindblad-span condition for Heisenberg scaling and optimal quantum-limit coefficients otherwise.
AI.motivation: Estimating a function of multiple Hamiltonian parameters is practically important, yet fundamental precision limits under Markovian noise were unclear. Prior work largely addressed estimating parameters individually, leaving open whether direct function estimation offers an advantage and what bounds govern Heisenberg versus standard quantum-limit scaling.
AI.method: The authors reduce multiparameter function estimation to an optimization over effective single-parameter embeddings, yielding tight bounds on the quantum Fisher information. They establish a necessary and sufficient Hamiltonian-not-in-Lindblad-span condition and construct a code that simultaneously cancels noise and nuisance Hamiltonian parameters while preserving the target signal. For the failing case, they apply approximate quantum error correction to attain the optimal coefficient.
AI.result: Tight quantum Fisher information bounds are obtained. When the condition holds, Heisenberg-limited scaling in time is achievable via the constructed code; when it fails, the optimal standard quantum-limit coefficient is derived and shown to be asymptotically attainable with approximate quantum error correction. Direct function estimation can substantially outperform estimating all parameters individually then evaluating the function, with the advantage scaling in both evolution time and number of parameters.
AI.conclusion: A sharp characterization of precision limits for multiparameter function estimation under Markovian noise is provided, identifying when Heisenberg scaling is possible and when it degrades to the standard quantum limit, and showing that direct function estimation yields scaling advantages.

title: Towards Surrogate Based Dequantization of Quantum Reinforcement Learning
summary: In recent years, the utility of parameterized quantum circuits as function approximators has been widely studied. In the context of reinforcement learning, this approach has led to variational quantum algorithms such as quantum Q-learning. While these methods show promising empirical results, and can provide provable advantages for artificial problems, it remains unclear whether they can provide a provable quantum advantage over classical approaches for problems of practical relevance. A natural way to investigate this question is through the lens of dequantization: The construction of efficient classical algorithms capable of matching the performance of quantum variational methods. Building on recent kernel-based dequantization results for supervised learning, we take steps towards extending this surrogate-based dequantization program to reinforcement learning. Specifically, we study the simplified setting of reinforcement learning with a uniform generative model in which uniformly random state-action samples are available, which models the regime of sampling from a large experience replay buffer after sufficient exploration. Within this setting, we provide finite sample guarantees for classical kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration, with classical kernels designed to match the inductive bias of particular parameterized quantum circuits. Using these results, we then provide a set of sufficient conditions, on the data-encoding strategy of a parameterized quantum circuit, the corresponding classical kernel, and the problem structure, under which kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration provides a meaningful dequantization of quantum Q-learning, in this simplified setting. Apart from providing rigorous dequantization guarantees when these conditions are met, these results also motivate the use of kernelized fitted Q-iteration as a dequantization heuristic when these sufficient conditions cannot be verified.

AI.tldr: The paper extends kernel-based dequantization from supervised learning to reinforcement learning, providing finite-sample guarantees for classical kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration in a uniform generative model. It gives sufficient conditions under which classical kernelized FQI matches quantum Q-learning, thereby dequantizing it in this simplified setting.
AI.motivation: Parameterized quantum circuits and variational quantum algorithms like quantum Q-learning show empirical promise and provable advantages on artificial problems, but it is unclear whether they offer a provable quantum advantage on practically relevant problems. Dequantization—constructing efficient classical algorithms matching quantum variational performance—is proposed as a natural lens to investigate this question.
AI.method: The authors study reinforcement learning with a uniform generative model (uniformly random state-action samples, modeling sampling from a large experience replay buffer after sufficient exploration). They analyze classical kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration using classical kernels designed to match the inductive bias of particular parameterized quantum circuits, building on recent kernel-based dequantization results for supervised learning.
AI.result: They provide finite sample guarantees for classical kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration in this setting. From these, they derive a set of sufficient conditions—on the data-encoding strategy of the parameterized quantum circuit, the corresponding classical kernel, and the problem structure—under which kernelized FQI yields a meaningful dequantization of quantum Q-learning.
AI.conclusion: When the sufficient conditions are met, the results provide rigorous dequantization guarantees; when they cannot be verified, the results motivate kernelized Fitted Q-Iteration as a practical dequantization heuristic.

title: Geometric View of Iterative Fixed-Node Dynamics
summary: The sign-structure of a quantum many-body ground state is a central quantity in fixed-node approaches to mitigating the Fermion sign problem. For continuum electronic-structure Hamiltonians, the correct sign-structure is sufficient to compute exact ground state properties; on the other hand, lattice fixed-node approaches retain an additional dependence on trial wave-function amplitudes which are improved upon non-optimally while preserving their sign structure. Here we consider an iterative map obtained by repeatedly replacing the fixed-node trial state with the ground state of its associated lattice fixed-node Hamiltonian (independent of whether and how a practical algorithm could implement this iteration). We show the fixed points of this map are eigenstates of the Hamiltonian and reduced Hamiltonian resulting in at most one fixed point in the interior of each sign chamber. We prove that the ground state fixed point is stable and that the boundary of the ground state sign chamber is repulsive. This shows the amplitude dependence beyond having the correct ground state sign-structure disappears under self-consistent iteration. In other sign chambers, energy descent can be obstructed by the imposed sign structure; this tension leads to the iteration driving select amplitudes to zero producing `support collapse' onto chamber boundaries and corresponding to reduced Hamiltonians. Excited-state fixed points are therefore provably unstable and flow toward lower-energy boundary fixed points. We show sign chamber boundaries have a directional stability; boundary points attractive in one direction are repulsive under a sign flip. By revealing the geometry and stability structure of iterative fixed-node dynamics, our results clarify the foundations of a central approach to the Fermion sign problem and motivate potential new algorithmic strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper studies an iterative fixed-node map that repeatedly replaces a trial state with the ground state of its associated lattice fixed-node Hamiltonian, and analyzes the geometry and stability of its fixed points.
AI.motivation: In continuum electronic-structure Hamiltonians, the correct sign-structure suffices to obtain exact ground-state properties, but lattice fixed-node methods retain an additional, non-optimally treated dependence on trial wave-function amplitudes (beyond their sign structure). The work aims to clarify whether and how this amplitude dependence is eliminated by self-consistency, and to understand the stability structure of iterative fixed-node dynamics as a foundation for the Fermion sign problem.
AI.method: The authors define and analyze an iterative map generated by repeatedly replacing the fixed-node trial state with the ground state of the associated lattice fixed-node Hamiltonian, independent of practical algorithmic realization. They characterize the fixed points, analyze behavior within and across sign chambers, and prove stability/repulsion properties, including directional stability of chamber boundaries under sign flips.
AI.result: Fixed points of the map are eigenstates of the Hamiltonian and reduced Hamiltonian, with at most one fixed point in the interior of each sign chamber. The ground-state fixed point is stable and the boundary of the ground-state sign chamber is repulsive. Amplitude dependence beyond the correct ground-state sign structure vanishes under self-consistent iteration. In other sign chambers, energy descent can be obstructed, driving selected amplitudes to zero, producing support collapse onto chamber boundaries described by reduced Hamiltonians. Excited-state fixed points are provably unstable and flow toward lower-energy boundary fixed points. Boundaries exhibit directional stability: points attractive in one direction are repulsive under a sign flip.
AI.conclusion: The geometry and stability structure of iterative fixed-node dynamics show that the ground-state fixed point is stable and that extra amplitude dependence disappears under self-consistent iteration, while excited-state fixed points are unstable. These results clarify the foundations of a central approach to the Fermion sign problem and motivate potential new algorithmic strategies.

title: qdmag: A Python package for simulating nonequilibrium magnetization of molecules using quantum master equations
summary: We present qdmag, a computational utility for calculating the magnetization of magnetic molecules in a time-varying external magnetic field by solving a generalized Lindblad quantum master equation with spin-phonon coupling treated as a dissipation term. The package relies on the spin Hamiltonian formalism, which includes both the magnetic exchange interactions and the zero-field splitting (ZFS) interaction. Different types of magnetic exchange interaction and ZFS terms up to 12th order, which are written in terms of the extended Stevens operators, are supported. qdmag enables long-time evolution of magnetization for up to a few milliseconds, which is achieved through a staircase approximation of the magnetic field as a function of time. For high-dimensional spin Hamiltonians, a lower-dimensional effective Hamiltonian is constructed to make the calculations computationally feasible. Three case studies of one-spin, two-spin, and three-spin systems are presented to demonstrate the usage of qdmag. Our work offers a computational tool to bridge the gap between theoretical development and numerical calculations of spin dynamics in the presence of spin-phonon coupling.

AI.tldr: qdmag is a computational package for simulating magnetization dynamics of magnetic molecules under time-varying magnetic fields, solving a generalized Lindblad master equation with spin-phonon coupling as dissipation.
AI.motivation: There is a gap between theoretical development and numerical calculations of spin dynamics when spin-phonon coupling is present, requiring a practical computational tool.
AI.method: Employs the spin Hamiltonian formalism including magnetic exchange and ZFS interactions (up to 12th order via extended Stevens operators). Solves a generalized Lindblad quantum master equation. Uses staircase approximation of the time-dependent field for long-time evolution (up to milliseconds) and constructs lower-dimensional effective Hamiltonians for high-dimensional spin systems.
AI.result: Demonstrated through three case studies: one-spin, two-spin, and three-spin systems. Enables magnetization evolution up to a few milliseconds.
AI.conclusion: qdmag provides a computational tool bridging theoretical and numerical studies of spin dynamics with spin-phonon coupling.

title: Pump-Free Microwave-Optical Bell Pair Generation for Teleportation-Based Quantum Transduction
summary: The coherent conversion between microwave and optical photons, known as quantum transduction, is critical for connecting superconducting processors to optical networks. Existing methods are limited by complications associated with optical pumping. We propose a pump-free microwave-optical Bell-pair source for teleportation-based transduction. Using a spin or atomic system resonantly coupled to optical and microwave cavities, the scheme generates loss-robust heralded Bell pairs. Across color centers, atomic ensembles, and phonon-mediated systems, this assembly achieves kilohertz-range heralding rates with high fidelity.

AI.tldr: A pump-free microwave-optical Bell-pair source enables teleportation-based quantum transduction, generating loss-robust heralded Bell pairs at kilohertz rates with high fidelity across spin, atomic, and phonon-mediated platforms.

title: Exact Work Characteristic Functions for Time-Dependent Bosonic Quadratic Hamiltonians
summary: We derive an exact analytical expression for the characteristic function of work in closed many-body bosonic systems governed by general time-dependent quadratic Hamiltonians. This is made possible by adopting a unified prescription in which all operators appearing in the characteristic function are treated as elements of the inhomogeneous Metaplectic group. The esulting expression involves a single symplectic matrix, a single phase-space displacement, and a single accumulated phase. It holds for any number of degrees of freedom, arbitrary time dependence of the quadratic Hamiltonian, and any initial thermal equilibrium state of the system. The formalism trades the explicit time-ordering problem associated with the unitary evolution for the determination of a symplectic path in phase space, from which the corresponding driving Hamiltonian can be reconstructed. We also discuss the generalization to arbitrary nonequilibrium initial states within the two-projective-measurement scheme for quantum work. The same construction yields Loschmidt echoes and mixed-state total phases. Using the derived characteristic function, we obtain formulas for the Helmholtz free energy, the Jarzynski equality, the mean work, the work variance, and the nonequilibrium lag. Undisplaced Hamiltonians, sudden quenches, constant-Hessian protocols, and the adiabatic limit follow as special cases of the general result. As an illustration, we analyze a one-dimensional system constructed from an unconventional symplectic path and exhibiting physically relevant limiting cases. We then show how affine and purely symplectic contributions affect work statistics and irreversibility.

title: Environmental records unlock universal quantum computation from thermal decoherence
summary: At a fixed thermal exposure, the same stabilizer processor can be classically simulable or quantum universal, depending on which environmental records its controller retains. We give an exact computational classification of energy-counting thermal-idle instruments in a quantum processor with ideal stabilizer control and independent local Markov baths. The relaxation time $T_1$, homogeneous coherence time $T_2$, and equilibrium excited-state population $p_e$ determine an exact computational boundary at $(1-p_e)T_2/T_1=1$. If every location lies at or below it, branchwise nonnegative stabilizer decompositions give an explicit efficient classical sampler for the adaptive circuit and its full time-resolved exchange record. Above it at a single repeatedly accessible location, a suitable idle duration and no-exchange conditioning supply distillable ancillas and enable universal quantum computation with polynomial overhead. At finite temperature on the resource side, erasing the record at a sufficiently long, unsplit exposure makes the averaged channel stabilizer measure-and-prepare, and even a terminal parity check then yields only simulable branches. Yet at that same exposure, retaining only the bit recording whether any exchange occurred still heralds distillable ancillas, because a thermal round trip restores the parity after its first exchange has already removed the coherence.
