AI.motivation: Whether a noisy quantum processor is classically simulable or quantum universal depends on the stabilizer dynamics and the retained environmental records. The paper aims to pinpoint the exact boundary between these regimes for a concrete, physically natural class of thermal-idle operations.
AI.method: The authors study energy-counting thermal-idle instruments with ideal stabilizer control and independent local Markov baths. They derive an exact computational boundary from relaxation time T1, homogeneous coherence time T2, and equilibrium excited-state population p_e, and construct branchwise nonnegative stabilizer decompositions for simulation and record-conditioned protocols for universality.

Below it, branchwise nonnegative stabilizer decompositions yield an explicit efficient classical sampler for the adaptive circuit and its full time-resolved exchange record. title: Error-Bounded Fixed-Point Design of Super-Sample-Rate IIR Filters for Real-Time Superconducting Qubit Flux Predistortion
summary: Flux-activated two-qubit gates in superconducting processors require correction of line distortion, which otherwise produces residual detuning, conditional-phase error, and leakage. Prior demonstrations of cryoscope-based distortion calibration have generally used commercial solutions that specify the filter models but not their FPGA implementation. These details matter for custom and open-source systems, where the fixed-point coefficient and datapath formats set how accurately the correction is realized, and the IIR feedback loop in its standard form does not meet timing at the required clock rate. We derive the coefficient formats of the correction filters from a step response error tolerance, using bounds on the quantization-induced displacement of the poles and zeros over the physical parameter range of each distortion, and the accumulator format from the smallest input change that must remain resolvable at the output. The same analysis gives the conditions under which quantization preserves filter stability. We implement the resulting FIR/IIR cascade on the QubiC platform at a fabric clock rate of \SI{500}{MHz}, using a super-sample-rate structure with scattered look-ahead pipelining, which removes the feedback recursion from the critical path without changing the target transfer function. A representative cascade for our \SI{1}{GS/s} flux lines, comprising an integrator, a second-order section, and a 20-tap FIR, consumes 88 DSP slices and adds \SI{162}{ns} of latency. We confirm the hardware implementation by correcting characteristic bias-tee distortion, an intermediate step toward full cryoscope-based calibration.

title: A complete classification of the existence of finite-dimensional quantum solutions to inconsistent linear constraint systems
summary:
Linear constraint systems (LCS) provide a compact algebraic language for nonlocal games and state-independent contextuality. In the binary case the Mermin--Peres square shows that inconsistent LCS can be solved by promoting variables to local Pauli operators, whereas a series of no-go results excludes analogous Pauli-, Clifford- and monomial unitary-based constructions at odd prime modulus. We first isolate the reason for this difference: for tensor-product quantum solutions, the obstruction to a classical solution of a LCS over $\mathbb{Z}_n$ decomposes into obstruction classes carried by the individual factors. As a consequence, a genuinely global obstruction cannot arise solely by tensoring locally unobstructed systems. The argument is specific to odd modulus; at even modulus the reordering phase need not vanish, as in Pauli-based examples.
  Given this distinction, we instead associate LCS to finite arrangements of rank-one projectors and resolutions of the identity in finite-dimensional vector spaces. Quantum solvability for such LCS is automatic and the search for a quantum-classical gap rests entirely on proving classical unsatisfiability of the underlying modular incidence problem of the arrangement. By relating such LCS with group-valued frame functions, we identify a family of examples in the work of [Harding, Jager, and Smith, Int. J. Theor. Phys. 44, 539 (2005)]. To establish the (non)existence of classically unsatisfiable LCS over $\mathbb{Z}_n$ with quantum solutions in all dimensions $d$ and for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, we further construct explicit examples for the cases $d=n$ prime. Our main result thus positively resolves the existence problem of such LCS beyond the binary case: such systems exist if and only if $d\geq 3$ and $\gcd(n,d)>1$. Moreover, we establish the existence of LCS with a quantum-classical gap over finite fields if and only if $d\geq 3$ and $p\mid d$.

AI.tldr: This paper studies quantum-classical gaps in linear constraint systems (LCS) over Z_n, showing the obstruction for tensor-product solutions decomposes into factor-wise classes for odd n, and then constructs LCS from rank-one projectors whose quantum solvability is automatic; the main result proves such LCS exist iff d >= 3 and gcd(n,d) > 1, with an analogous finite-field criterion.
AI.motivation: The Mermin-Peres square shows inconsistent binary LCS admit quantum (Pauli) solutions, while no-go results exclude analogous Clifford/monomial constructions at odd prime modulus. The paper aims to explain this asymmetry and to resolve whether classically unsatisfiable LCS with quantum solutions exist beyond the binary case, for all dimensions and all moduli.
AI.method: First, analyze tensor-product quantum solutions over Z_n and decompose the classical-solution obstruction into obstruction classes carried by individual tensor factors, isolating why the obstruction is only global at odd modulus due to vanishing reordering phase. Second, associate LCS to finite arrangements of rank-one projectors and resolutions of the identity, relate them to group-valued frame functions, and construct explicit examples for cases d = n prime using known examples of Harding, Jager, and Smith.
AI.result: For odd modulus, a genuinely global obstruction cannot arise solely by tensoring locally unobstructed systems, since the obstruction decomposes factor-wise; at even modulus the reordering phase need not vanish. The main result positively resolves the existence problem: classically unsatisfiable LCS over Z_n with quantum solutions exist if and only if d >= 3 and gcd(n,d) > 1. Moreover, LCS with a quantum-classical gap over finite fields exist if and only if d >= 3 and p | d.
AI.conclusion: The paper characterizes exactly when classically unsatisfiable LCS with quantum solutions exist, extending beyond the binary case to all dimensions d and all n: the condition is d >= 3 and gcd(n,d) > 1 (and d >= 3 with p | d over finite fields). This settles the existence problem and clarifies the structural origin of quantum-classical gaps via factor-wise obstruction decomposition.

title: Exact Ionization Amplitudes for a Delta-Function Well in an Arbitrary-Strength DC Electric Field
summary: We investigate finite-time field-induced ionization from a one-dimensional attractive delta-function well in a uniform dc electric field of arbitrary strength. Our aim is to determine the physical bound-state survival amplitude \(a_b(t)\) at any observation time without constructing the complete time-dependent propagator or wavefunction. In the gauge-equivalent Kramers--Henneberger representation, the field appears as motion of the contact point, and the resulting dynamics reduces to a closed Volterra equation. Exact endpoint-phase factorization organizes the full chronological rescattering history into a relative-time convolution hierarchy and an exact resolvent. By introducing the accumulated bound-state amplitude and reorganizing its two-time domain in relative and complementary center times, the final contact contribution becomes an explicit boundary integral. All spatial integrations are carried out analytically. The field-driven contact-free term is obtained in closed form using the Faddeeva function, while the direct and repeated-rescattering terms are expressed as explicitly evaluable time integrals. The result applies at arbitrary dc-field strength and finite time, with no weak-field expansion, rescattering truncation, or asymptotic-time approximation. It is verified through the exact field-free limit and an independent numerical solution of the original physical Volterra equation. The formulation gives an exact nonperturbative solution of a fundamental ionization model and reveals otherwise hidden analytical structure in driven quantum dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an exact, nonperturbative finite-time bound-state survival amplitude for a 1D attractive delta-function well under an arbitrary-strength uniform dc electric field, using the Kramers-Henneberger frame and a closed Volterra equation with endpoint-phase factorization.
AI.motivation: The goal is to obtain the physical bound-state survival amplitude a_b(t) at any finite observation time without constructing the full time-dependent propagator or wavefunction, and without relying on weak-field expansions, rescattering truncations, or asymptotic-time approximations.
AI.method: In the gauge-equivalent Kramers-Henneberger representation, the field becomes motion of the contact point, reducing the dynamics to a closed Volterra equation. Exact endpoint-phase factorization organizes the chronological rescattering history into a relative-time convolution hierarchy with an exact resolvent. By introducing the accumulated bound-state amplitude and reorganizing its two-time domain into relative and complementary center times, the final contact contribution becomes an explicit boundary integral. All spatial integrations are performed analytically; the field-driven contact-free term is expressed via the Faddeeva function, and direct and repeated-rescattering terms become explicitly evaluable time integrals.
AI.result: The formulation yields a closed-form, explicitly evaluable expression for the survival amplitude valid at arbitrary dc-field strength and finite time, verified against the exact field-free limit and an independent numerical solution of the original physical Volterra equation.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an exact nonperturbative solution of a fundamental ionization model and uncovers hidden analytical structure in driven quantum dynamics.

title: Truncated hybrid tensor networks for distributed quantum simulation
summary: Simulation of quantum many-body systems is a principal application of quantum computing, but available devices remain limited by the number of qubits and cannot accommodate systems of the desired size. One approach is to host a large evolution across several modest distributed systems that exchange classical information alone. Current protocols such as circuit knitting incur a quasi-probability sampling cost that grows exponentially with the number of remote gates across the cut, even when physical correlations across the cut are actually bounded. In this work, we present a truncated hybrid tensor network (THTN) framework in which a remote two-body gate is applied as a sum of local unitaries on the subsystems, linked by a classical connecting tensor, and an interface truncation retains Schmidt modes across the cut. Remote gates between the same subsystems can be merged on one connector, so non-one-dimensional models, such as layered partitions with strong intra-layer and weaker interlayer couplings, may be cast onto a one-dimensional cut. The retained non-negative Schmidt coefficients also define a sampling rule for local observables. We validate this distributed protocol by classical simulation against time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) at the same bond dimension. The truncated dynamics track the TEBD references on chains and ladders, with the clearest gain on a layered model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a truncated hybrid tensor network (THTN) framework for distributed quantum simulation of many-body systems. Remote two-body gates are decomposed into local unitaries linked by a classical connecting tensor, with interface truncation retaining Schmidt modes across the cut. Unlike circuit knitting, the method avoids exponential quasi-probability sampling overhead, merging remote gates onto a single connector and mapping non-1D models onto 1D cuts. Classical simulation against TEBD validates the protocol.
AI.motivation: Quantum many-body simulation is a key quantum computing application, but current devices are limited by qubit count and cannot host systems of the desired size. Distributed approaches exchanging only classical information are promising, yet existing protocols such as circuit knitting suffer from a quasi-probability sampling cost that grows exponentially with the number of remote gates across the cut—even when physical correlations across the cut are actually bounded.
AI.method: A truncated hybrid tensor network (THTN) framework is proposed in which a remote two-body gate is applied as a sum of local unitaries on subsystems, connected by a classical connecting tensor, with an interface truncation that retains Schmidt modes across the cut. Remote gates between the same subsystems are merged onto one connector, allowing non-1D models (e.g., layered partitions with strong intra-layer and weaker interlayer couplings) to be cast onto a 1D cut. The retained non-negative Schmidt coefficients define a sampling rule for local observables.
AI.result: The distributed protocol was validated by classical simulation against time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) at the same bond dimension. The truncated dynamics track the TEBD references on chains and ladders, with the clearest gain observed on a layered model.
AI.conclusion: THTN enables distributed quantum simulation with a cut cost tied to physical correlations rather than the number of remote gates, avoiding the exponential quasi-probability overhead of circuit knitting. It accurately reproduces TEBD dynamics on chains, ladders, and layered models, offering an effective approach for simulating systems larger than any single device can accommodate.

title: Phantom Codes: Hardness, Rate Optimal qLDPC Constructions, and Distance Limits
summary:
An $[[n,k,d]]$ stabilizer code is phantom if every in-block logical CNOT gate can be realized by a permutation of its physical qubits. This eliminates the large and complicated physical overhead normally required for logical entangling gates. Yet this symmetry is highly restrictive: phantom codes are rare, the number of logical qubits is limited to $k=O(\log n)$, and no phantom qLDPC family with growing logical dimension was previously known.
  We make three contributions.
  1. We prove that recognizing phantomness of a given stabilizer code is at least as hard as Graph Isomorphism, even for CSS codes encoding only $k=2$ logical qubits.
  2. We propose the first rate optimal phantom qLDPC families: for every fixed $D$, our CSS families achieve the maximal logical scaling $k=Θ(\log n)$ and distance $d\geq D$.
  3. We prove a distance no-go theorem: every phantom code family with $k=ω(\sqrt{\log n})$ and check weight $w=O(1)$ satisfies $d\leq w$ for sufficiently large $n$.
  Thus our fixed-distance qLDPC families are distance-scaling optimal at the maximal logical scaling $k=Θ(\log n)$.

AI.tldr: This paper studies phantom stabilizer codes, whose in-block logical CNOT gates are realized by physical-qubit permutations, eliminating entangling-gate overhead. It shows phantomness recognition is as hard as Graph Isomorphism, constructs the first rate-optimal phantom qLDPC families achieving k=Θ(log n) with fixed distance, and proves a distance no-go theorem bounding distance for phantom codes with k=ω(√log n).
AI.motivation: Logical entangling gates such as CNOT normally demand large and complicated physical overhead. Phantom codes avoid this by realizing in-block logical CNOTs via permutations of physical qubits, but the symmetry is restrictive: phantom codes are rare, k is limited to O(log n), and no phantom qLDPC family with growing logical dimension was previously known. The paper aims to characterize the complexity of phantomness recognition and to construct phantom qLDPC families that attain the maximal logical scaling.
AI.method: The authors (1) reduce Graph Isomorphism to the problem of recognizing whether a given stabilizer code is phantom, even for CSS codes with only k=2 logical qubits; (2) construct CSS phantom qLDPC families, for every fixed D, that achieve k=Θ(log n) and distance d≥D; and (3) prove a distance no-go theorem for phantom code families with k=ω(√log n) and constant check weight w=O(1), showing d≤w for sufficiently large n.
AI.result: Phantomness recognition is at least as hard as Graph Isomorphism, even for CSS codes with k=2. The first rate-optimal phantom qLDPC families are constructed, achieving maximal logical scaling k=Θ(log n) with distance d≥D for every fixed D. A no-go theorem shows that phantom families with k=ω(√log n) and check weight w=O(1) must have d≤w for large n.
AI.conclusion: Phantom codes enable permutation-realized logical CNOTs but impose strict constraints. The constructed fixed-distance qLDPC families are distance-scaling optimal at the maximal logical scaling k=Θ(log n). Together with the hardness result and the distance no-go theorem, the paper delineates both the computational complexity and the performance limits of phantom stabilizer codes.

title: Partial projected ensembles reveal slow tilt-constrained information spreading
summary: Projected ensembles reveal information about quantum many-body dynamics beyond the reduced density matrix. Here we investigate how spatial constraints affect the emergence of this information in a kicked Ising chain with a spatially varying longitudinal field. We consider partial projected ensembles, obtained by measuring a remote region while leaving an intervening buffer unobserved. Our numerical results reveal a pronounced contrast between nearly ballistic correlation onset in the ergodic regime and strongly delayed onset in the tilt-constrained regime, corroborated by quantum mutual information. Despite these different onset scales, the conditional-state fluctuations decrease approximately exponentially with buffer length in both regimes. Full projected ensembles additionally exhibit slow relaxation and persistent measurement-basis dependence in their higher moments. We establish an information-theoretic characterization of the connected second moment and use a solvable dephasing model with effective-basis measurements to illustrate the separation of phase accumulation and coherence loss. Within this model, a factorially suppressed coupling envelope yields sublogarithmic spreading consistent with the finite-distance onset trends. Our results identify partial projected ensembles as probes of the distinction between the time required for correlations to develop and the information that remains accessible under partial observation.

AI.tldr: This work studies how spatial constraints and a spatially varying longitudinal field affect information in projected ensembles of a kicked Ising chain, revealing distinct correlation-onset regimes and exponential decay of conditional-state fluctuations with buffer length.
AI.motivation: Projected ensembles encode information about quantum many-body dynamics that goes beyond the reduced density matrix, but how spatial constraints govern the emergence and accessibility of this information—particularly under partial observation with an unobserved buffer region—remains insufficiently understood.
AI.method: The authors analyze a kicked Ising chain with a spatially varying longitudinal field, computing partial projected ensembles by measuring a remote region while leaving an intervening buffer unobserved. They compare an ergodic regime with a tilt-constrained regime, supplement the analysis with quantum mutual information, characterize the connected second moment information-theoretically, and introduce a solvable dephasing model with effective-basis measurements to separate phase accumulation from coherence loss.

Yet conditional-state fluctuations decay approximately exponentially with buffer length in both regimes. Full projected ensembles display slow relaxation and persistent measurement-basis dependence in higher moments. The solvable dephasing model, featuring a factorially suppressed coupling envelope, yields sublogarithmic spreading that matches the finite-distance onset trends.
AI.conclusion: Partial projected ensembles serve as effective probes distinguishing the time needed for correlations to develop from the information that remains accessible under partial observation, with spatial constraints strongly shaping the latter.

title: Pretty good quantum state transfer via transcendental edge weights
summary: We prove that if we take a rooted product of a circulant graph with universal perfect state transfer with a path of fixed length whose end edge is weighted with a transcendental number, then there is pretty good state transfer between any pair of endpoints of these paths. As a consequence, in a path with an even number of vertices with transcendental weights on the two edges incident to the endpoints, there is pretty good state transfer.

AI.tldr: Rooted products of circulant graphs (with universal perfect state transfer) and fixed-length paths—where the end edge carries a transcendental weight—exhibit pretty good state transfer between any pair of path endpoints; consequently, even-vertex paths with transcendental weights on the two endpoint-incident edges admit pretty good state transfer.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to construct and characterize new families of graphs exhibiting pretty good state transfer (PGST), extending known results on perfect state transfer in circulant graphs via the rooted product operation, and to exploit transcendental edge weights as a device to guarantee PGST.
AI.method: The authors use the rooted product of a circulant graph possessing universal perfect state transfer with a fixed-length path whose terminal edge is assigned a transcendental weight, then analyze the resulting spectral/eigenvector structure to establish PGST between path endpoints; the argument is then specialized to even-order weighted paths.
AI.result: It is proven that in such rooted products there is pretty good state transfer between any pair of endpoints of the paths; as a corollary, a path on an even number of vertices with transcendental weights on the two edges incident to its endpoints also admits pretty good state transfer.
AI.conclusion: Transcendental edge weights, combined with rooted products of circulant graphs having universal perfect state transfer, yield a general mechanism for producing pretty good state transfer, with weighted even paths as a concrete consequence.

title: Strong converse for the quantum capacity of the pure-loss bosonic channel
summary: This paper reports the proof of a strong converse for the unconstrained quantum capacity of the pure-loss bosonic channel. At every fixed rate above capacity, the entanglement-generation fidelity of every code is bounded by a constant times the reciprocal of the number of channel uses. The bound holds without an energy constraint and for arbitrary encoded states, including states correlated across all input modes, and arbitrary joint decoders. The proof combines quantum Chebyshev and hockey-stick testing inequalities with a uniform relative-entropy-variance bound for the balanced pure-loss channel, corresponding to transmissivity $η=1/2$. The variance bound follows by expressing the balanced beam splitter in bright and dark modes: the dark modes are exactly in vacuum, and any state orthogonal to that vacuum contains at least one dark photon. For general transmissivity, dilating the degrading attenuator reduces the problem to this balanced-channel setting and bounds the decoder test by precisely the factor that produces the known quantum-capacity threshold. The resulting argument establishes the strong converse at the unconstrained quantum capacity for every pure-loss bosonic channel.

AI.motivation: The unconstrained quantum capacity of pure-loss bosonic channels was known, but a strong converse—ruling out any nonzero fidelity at rates above capacity for arbitrary states and decoders—had not been established. Proving it is needed to fully characterize the operational limits of these channels without energy constraints.

For general transmissivity, the degrading attenuator is dilated to reduce the problem to the balanced-channel setting, and the decoder test is bounded by precisely the factor yielding the known quantum-capacity threshold.

The bound holds without an energy constraint, for arbitrary encoded states—including states correlated across all input modes—and for arbitrary joint decoders.

title: Floquet Dressing and Bath Spectral Effects on the Geometric Phase of a Driven Dissipative Qubit
summary: Building on recent work by Wang et al. on the dissipative geometric phase (GP) in the spin-boson model (SBM), the GP dynamics of a periodically driven symmetric SBM are investigated using the numerically exact process-tensor time-evolving matrix product operator (PT-TEMPO) method. A symmetric two-level system subjected to a longitudinal monochromatic drive along the same system coordinate that couples to an Ohmic bosonic environment exhibits rich GP dynamics arising from the interplay between driving and dissipation. To isolate cooperative drive-bath effects, a non-additive GP contribution is introduced that separates the driven dissipative response from its driven-unitary and undriven-dissipative components. Periodic driving is found to either suppress or enhance bath-induced GP deformation depending on the interplay between drive and bath timescales. These trends are interpreted through Floquet spectral steering, whereby the drive redistributes the coherent dynamics among quasienergy sidebands whose transition frequencies and Fourier-resolved system-bath matrix elements determine their coupling to the environmental spectrum. Floquet analysis shows that the dominant dissipative pathways are governed jointly by Floquet matrix-element weights and bath spectral overlap, rather than by either alone. These results connect Floquet engineering, quantum dissipation, and GP dynamics and establish periodic driving as a means of controlling the GP of open quantum systems (OQSs).

AI.tldr: This work studies the dissipative geometric phase (GP) of a periodically driven symmetric spin-boson model using the numerically exact PT-TEMPO method, showing that Floquet spectral steering lets driving suppress or enhance bath-induced GP deformation depending on drive-bath timescale interplay.
AI.motivation: Building on Wang et al.'s work on the dissipative GP in the spin-boson model, the authors aim to understand how periodic driving reshapes GP dynamics in an open quantum system, and whether driving can serve as a control knob for GP in the presence of dissipation.
AI.method: A symmetric two-level system is driven longitudinally by a monochromatic field along the same coordinate that couples to an Ohmic bosonic bath. The GP dynamics are computed with the numerically exact PT-TEMPO method. A non-additive GP contribution is defined to subtract the driven-unitary and undriven-dissipative components, isolating cooperative drive-bath effects. Floquet analysis links the trends to quasienergy sidebands, Floquet matrix-element weights, and bath spectral overlap.
AI.result: Periodic driving can either suppress or enhance bath-induced GP deformation depending on the interplay of drive and bath timescales. Floquet analysis shows the dominant dissipative pathways are jointly determined by Floquet matrix-element weights and bath spectral overlap, not by either factor alone.
AI.conclusion: The results connect Floquet engineering, quantum dissipation, and GP dynamics, establishing periodic driving as a means of controlling the GP of open quantum systems.

title: Quantum Simulation of Two-Dimensional Free Dirac Hamiltonian in Multimode Circuit QED
summary: Two-dimensional massive Dirac systems feature a gapped Dirac-cone dispersion central to a broad range of phenomena in condensed-matter and topological physics. While quantum simulations have demonstrated one-dimensional Dirac dynamics and two-dimensional massless Weyl dynamics, programmable simulation of massive two-dimensional Dirac dynamics remains experimentally unexplored. Here, we realize a programmable two-dimensional free Dirac Hamiltonian in circuit QED, with independently tunable spin-momentum couplings and mass, using a single Rabi-driven qubit coupled to two modes of a multimode cavity. Using this Hamiltonian, we observe rotational Zitterbewegung of a two-dimensional massive Dirac particle and its dependence on the effective mass. Time-dependent master-equation simulations incorporating measured decoherence, corrections beyond the rotating-wave approximation (RWA), and anharmonicity of the transmon reproduce the observed dynamics. Our results establish multimode circuit QED as a compact, programmable platform for higher-dimensional relativistic quantum dynamics and provide a foundation for exploring dynamical and topological phenomena in gapped Dirac systems.

AI.tldr: A programmable 2D free massive Dirac Hamiltonian is realized in circuit QED using a single Rabi-driven qubit coupled to two cavity modes, enabling observation of rotational Zitterbewegung and its mass dependence.
AI.motivation: Two-dimensional massive Dirac systems are central to condensed-matter and topological physics, but while 1D Dirac and 2D massless Weyl dynamics have been quantum-simulated, programmable simulation of 2D massive Dirac dynamics remained experimentally unexplored.
AI.method: The authors engineer a 2D free Dirac Hamiltonian in circuit QED with independently tunable spin-momentum couplings and mass, implemented via a single Rabi-driven qubit coupled to two modes of a multimode cavity. Time-dependent master-equation simulations include measured decoherence, beyond-RWA corrections, and transmon anharmonicity.
AI.result: Rotational Zitterbewegung of a 2D massive Dirac particle and its dependence on effective mass were observed. Simulations incorporating decoherence, beyond-RWA corrections, and transmon anharmonicity reproduce the observed dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Multimode circuit QED is established as a compact, programmable platform for higher-dimensional relativistic quantum dynamics, providing a foundation for exploring dynamical and topological phenomena in gapped Dirac systems.

title: Two-qubit gates for the soft 0-π qubit
summary: The 0-π qubit promises longer lifetimes than the transmon, making it a strong candidate for a next-generation, lower-error qubit. Gyenis et al. experimentally demonstrated an unprotected single-qubit gate in the soft 0-π regime [1], but no corresponding two-qubit gate has yet been proposed. We propose an unprotected CZ gate for capacitively coupled soft 0-π qubits. The gate uses a direct transition between a computational state and a higher non-computational state. Assuming negligible device disorder and a phenomenological noise model, the simulated CZ gate achieves a fidelity of approximately 99.9% at a gate time of approximately 160 ns.

AI.tldr: Proposes an unprotected CZ gate for capacitively coupled soft 0-π qubits via a direct transition to a non-computational state, achieving ~99.9% fidelity in ~160 ns.
AI.motivation: The 0-π qubit promises longer lifetimes and lower errors than the transmon, and while a single-qubit gate has been demonstrated, no two-qubit gate had been proposed for the soft 0-π regime.
AI.method: An unprotected CZ gate for capacitively coupled soft 0-π qubits exploiting a direct transition between a computational state and a higher non-computational state, evaluated with simulations under a phenomenological noise model and negligible device disorder.
AI.result: The simulated CZ gate achieves a fidelity of approximately 99.9% at a gate time of approximately 160 ns.
AI.conclusion: The proposed gate provides the missing two-qubit counterpart for soft 0-π qubits, indicating their potential as next-generation lower-error qubits.

title: Approximate synthesis of general single-qubit unitaries over the Clifford+$\sqrt{T}$ gate set
summary: For the standard Clifford+$T$ gate set, deterministic, ancilla-free synthesis now attains the minimal $T$-count for general single-qubit unitaries (Morisaki et al., arXiv:2510.05816). The $\sqrt{T}$ gate rotates by half the angle of $T$, generating a finer lattice of implementable operations. It was assumed that access to this magic state lowers the cost of deterministic and ancilla-free synthesis of general single-qubit unitaries, but no direct Clifford+$\sqrt{T}$ algorithm existed for this case. We provide one by extending the integer lattice-point enumeration method of Morisaki et al. We adopt a resource state cost model based on the magic-state catalysis approach of Gidney and Fowler (arXiv:1812.01238). On Haar-random targets synthesized to precisions ranging from $\varepsilon=10^{-3}$ to $10^{-8}$, the cost of Clifford+$\sqrt{T}$ circuits scales as $2.4\log_2(1/\varepsilon)$ compared to $3.0\log_2(1/\varepsilon)$ for the provably $T$-count-optimal Clifford+$T$ circuits. Once a one-time catalyst state is amortized, the Clifford+$\sqrt{T}$ circuits are never costlier than their Clifford+$T$ counterparts.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first direct Clifford+√T algorithm for deterministic, ancilla-free synthesis of general single-qubit unitaries by extending an integer lattice-point enumeration method, achieving lower asymptotic cost than Clifford+T.
AI.motivation: Deterministic, ancilla-free Clifford+T synthesis attains minimal T-count, but the √T gate (rotating by half the T angle) offers a finer implementable lattice. It was assumed that √T magic-state access would reduce synthesis cost, but no direct Clifford+√T synthesis algorithm for general single-qubit unitaries existed.
AI.method: The authors extend the integer lattice-point enumeration method of Morisaki et al. (arXiv:2510.05816) to the Clifford+√T gate set, and adopt a resource-state cost model based on the magic-state catalysis approach of Gidney and Fowler (arXiv:1812.01238).
AI.result: On Haar-random targets synthesized to precisions ε = 10^-3 to 10^-8, Clifford+√T circuit cost scales as 2.4 log2(1/ε), versus 3.0 log2(1/ε) for provably T-count-optimal Clifford+T circuits. Once the one-time catalyst state is amortized, Clifford+√T circuits are never costlier than their Clifford+T counterparts.
AI.conclusion: A direct Clifford+√T synthesis algorithm yields asymptotically cheaper deterministic, ancilla-free single-qubit unitary synthesis than optimal Clifford+T, with a one-time catalyst amortization eliminating any cost disadvantage.

title: Phase Transition in Binary Compressed Sensing via Annealing with Adaptive Regularization
summary: Regularization choice changes the recovery phase diagrams of annealing-based binary compressed sensing. We develop a regularization-selection method that combines systematic parameter search with random forest regression. Under noiseless Gaussian measurements with known sparsity, reference parameters are selected from a candidate grid by minimizing mean squared reconstruction error over repeated simulated annealing (SA) trials. The fitted model predicts these reference values from signal dimension, sampling ratio, and sparsity. With predicted regularization, the SA recovery transition broadly follows the asymptotic reference boundary for box-constrained $\ell_1$ recovery at the larger signal dimensions examined. Without retraining, the same predictor supplies identical regularization values to SA and a quantum--classical hybrid solver. On matched problem instances, the hybrid solver yields smaller mean squared reconstruction errors than SA in parts of the evaluated parameter space. The resulting rule reuses the searched information for subsequent reconstruction without repeating candidate searches at each setting. The results quantify empirical performance under the stated finite candidate grid and solver settings; they do not constitute a solver-independent recovery guarantee or a time-to-solution comparison.

AI.tldr: A random-forest-based regularization-selection method is developed for annealing-based binary compressed sensing, enabling parameter reuse across annealing schedules and a quantum-classical hybrid solver.
AI.motivation: Regularization choice shifts the recovery phase diagrams of annealing-based binary compressed sensing, motivating a systematic way to select regularization parameters instead of relying on ad hoc choices.
AI.method: Reference regularization parameters are selected from a candidate grid by minimizing mean squared reconstruction error over repeated simulated annealing trials under noiseless Gaussian measurements with known sparsity. A random forest is fitted to predict these reference values from signal dimension, sampling ratio, and sparsity. The predictor is then applied without retraining to both SA and a quantum-classical hybrid solver.
AI.result: With predicted regularization, the SA recovery transition broadly follows the asymptotic reference boundary for box-constrained l1 recovery at larger signal dimensions. On matched instances, the hybrid solver achieves smaller mean squared reconstruction errors than SA in parts of the evaluated parameter space.
AI.conclusion: The resulting rule reuses searched information for subsequent reconstruction without repeating candidate searches per setting. Findings quantify empirical performance under the stated finite candidate grid and solver settings, and do not constitute a solver-independent recovery guarantee or time-to-solution comparison.

title: Improved Separations between Quantum and Classical Communication Complexity of Total Functions
summary: We refine Gavinsky's framework (arXiv:2608.18784) for exponential separations between quantum and randomized communication complexity of total functions and obtain larger separations: polylogarithmic quantum communication versus $\tildeΩ(\sqrt n)$ randomized communication with two quantum messages, and versus $Ω(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$ with more quantum messages.

AI.tldr: This work sharpens Gavinsky's framework for exponential quantum-vs-randomized communication separations for total functions, achieving polylogarithmic quantum communication against $\tilde\Omega(\sqrt n)$ randomized communication with two quantum messages, and against $\Omega(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ with more messages.
AI.motivation: Prior work (Gavinsky, arXiv:2608.18784) established a framework for exponential separations between quantum and randomized communication complexity of total functions. This paper aims to strengthen that framework to obtain larger separations.
AI.method: The authors refine Gavinsky's framework for constructing total functions exhibiting exponential separations between quantum and randomized communication complexity, controlling the number of quantum messages used in the protocol.
AI.result: They achieve polylogarithmic quantum communication versus $\tilde\Omega(\sqrt n)$ randomized communication with two quantum messages, and polylogarithmic quantum communication versus $\Omega(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ randomized communication (for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$) when more quantum messages are allowed.
AI.conclusion: Refining Gavinsky's framework yields larger exponential separations for total functions, with the trade-off that stronger randomized lower bounds require additional quantum messages.

title: Experimental Private Quantum Networked Sensing
summary: Entangling distant quantum sensors is a key application of future quantum networks, allowing for the estimation of global functions of local parameters, with precision that is not possible with stand-alone, individual, quantum sensors. However, with this advantage comes the risk of information leakage over the network via possible malicious parties. It is often particularly important that local parameters remain unknown and that only the global function is shared across the network. Recently, the notion of privacy has been introduced in this context, which ensures that only the agreed function of parameters is shared over the network, even when malicious parties control the network itself, whilst maintaining the estimation advantage. In this work, we introduce a noise-robust protocol for private quantum networked sensing, which we realise using a high-fidelity Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state source. We further run a comparative analysis and simulate attacks using three different quantum states, a four-qubit GHZ state, two Bell pairs, and a fully separable state. Our results highlight the clear advantage of GHZ states in maintaining high precision, accuracy, and privacy for the distributed estimation task.

AI.tldr: This work introduces a noise-robust protocol for private quantum networked sensing, realized with a high-fidelity GHZ state source, and shows via comparative analysis and simulated attacks that GHZ states outperform two Bell pairs and a fully separable state in precision, accuracy, and privacy for distributed estimation.
AI.motivation: Entangling distant quantum sensors enables estimation of global functions of local parameters beyond the precision of stand-alone sensors, but this advantage introduces a risk of information leakage over the network via malicious parties. In many settings it is essential that local parameters remain unknown and only the agreed global function is shared, so privacy must be guaranteed even when adversaries control the network, while still preserving the estimation advantage.
AI.method: The authors introduce a noise-robust protocol for private quantum networked sensing and realize it using a high-fidelity Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state source. They perform a comparative analysis and simulate attacks using three different quantum states: a four-qubit GHZ state, two Bell pairs, and a fully separable state.
AI.result: The comparative analysis and simulated attacks show a clear advantage of GHZ states in maintaining high precision, accuracy, and privacy for the distributed estimation task relative to two Bell pairs and a fully separable state.
AI.conclusion: GHZ states, combined with the proposed noise-robust private networked sensing protocol, offer a superior route to private distributed quantum sensing, outperforming Bell-pair and separable-state alternatives across precision, accuracy, and privacy.

title: Initial-Slip Dynamics Enables the Quantum Mpemba Effect
comment: Main: 10 pages, 4 figures. Supplemental Material: 24 pages, 1 figure
summary: We investigate the quantum Mpemba effect, whereby a system initially farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one initially closer to equilibrium, emerging in a quantum harmonic oscillator linearly coupled to a bosonic environment. Starting from factorized thermal states at different temperatures, we derive exact analytical criteria for the occurrence of the quantum Mpemba effect valid also beyond the typically considered weak-coupling and Markovian approximations. Most importantly, we show that the effect is enabled by the initial-slip dynamics generated by the sudden switch-on of the system-bath interaction. Neglecting this contribution completely suppresses the anomalous relaxation, identifying transient system-bath correlations as the key ingredient underlying the quantum Mpemba effect.

AI.tldr: The quantum Mpemba effect is shown to emerge in a quantum harmonic oscillator linearly coupled to a bosonic bath, enabled by initial-slip dynamics and transient system-bath correlations.
AI.motivation: The quantum Mpemba effect—where a system farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one closer to it—is counterintuitive and its physical origin is not fully understood. The authors aim to identify the key mechanism underlying this anomalous relaxation using a solvable open quantum system.
AI.method: A quantum harmonic oscillator linearly coupled to a bosonic environment is studied. Starting from factorized thermal states at different temperatures, the authors derive exact analytical criteria for the emergence of the quantum Mpemba effect, valid beyond the weak-coupling and Markovian approximations. They analyze the role of initial-slip dynamics induced by the sudden switch-on of the system-bath interaction.
AI.result: Exact analytical criteria for the quantum Mpemba effect are obtained, applicable beyond weak-coupling and Markovian regimes. The effect is shown to be enabled by initial-slip dynamics; neglecting this contribution completely suppresses the anomalous relaxation.
AI.conclusion: Transient system-bath correlations generated by the sudden switch-on of the interaction are identified as the key ingredient underlying the quantum Mpemba effect.

title: TSS Graphs for Hadamard Matrices: Real vs Complex
summary:
We have observed that Hadamard matrices whether real or complex lead to a dense output of identical probabilities for any given single input state. Complex Hadamard matrices have unusual orders and introduce phase which prove useful when controlled phase transformation gates are used. By taking a superposed combinations of input states, we discovered that the Hadamards generate non-uniform probabilities which is practically significant towards amplitude amplification without the need for manual parameterization like Grover's operator~\cite{grover1996}. A variety of graph theoretic properties are applied to TSS graphs and their trends were explored. Additionally, graphs turn out to be nearly isomorphic for the same set of input states which has potential applications for developing Quantum Algorithms.
  Keywords: Quantum Algorithms, Hadamard Matrices, Unitary Matrix Approach, Topological Structure of Superpositions (TSS), Graph Theory

AI.tldr: Hadamard matrices (real or complex) produce dense uniform probabilities for single input states, but superposed input states yield non-uniform probabilities, enabling amplitude amplification without manual parameterization.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to leverage the distinct behaviors of real and complex Hadamard matrices—particularly their unusual orders and phase introduction—to achieve amplitude amplification without the need for manual parameterization like Grover's operator, and to explore graph-theoretic properties for quantum algorithm development.
AI.method: The authors analyze Hadamard matrices (real and complex) in the context of quantum algorithms using a unitary matrix approach. They examine single versus superposed input states, apply graph-theoretic properties to Topological Structure of Superpositions (TSS) graphs, and investigate trends and near-isomorphism among graphs for identical input sets.
AI.result: Single input states produce dense, identical probability outputs. Superposed input states generate non-uniform probabilities that are practically significant for amplitude amplification. Graph-theoretic analysis of TSS graphs reveals trends and near-isomorphism for the same input states.
AI.conclusion: Hadamard matrices enable amplitude amplification via superposed input states without manual parameterization. TSS graph properties, including near-isomorphism, have potential applications for developing quantum algorithms.

title: Understanding the spin coherence of molecular photoexcited triplet states from first principles
summary: Optically readable molecular spins are attractive as quantum sensors due to their nanoscale modularity, synthetic tunability, and scope for sensitive readout. In particular, photoexcited spin-triplet states in organic molecules are appealing in supporting high optical-spin contrast at room temperature. Their utility is underpinned by their coherence, which warrants a detailed understanding of it. Here, from first principles, we systematically explore the Hahn-echo decoherence of the benchmark molecular system for room-temperature optically detected spin coherence---pentacene guest molecules coupled to a para-terphenyl host. Using generalized cluster-correlation expansion methods, we investigate the mechanisms of nuclear-spin-induced decoherence from zero to high magnetic field, exploring the role of guest vs host molecules, specific nuclei, zero-field splitting interactions, and hyperfine parameters. We describe how zero-field decoherence is driven by ~6 nuclei on the guest, while high-field decoherence is driven by ~600 nuclei in the host; how the longitudinal zero-field splitting parameter, $D$, can prolong $T_2$; and the magnetic-field-dependent processes which drive decoherence. These results advance our understanding of decoherence in optically readable molecular spins, providing insight for their synthetic enhancement and deployment as quantum probes.

AI.tldr: This work uses first-principles generalized cluster-correlation expansion to dissect Hahn-echo decoherence in pentacene-in-para-terphenyl, revealing distinct nuclear-spin-driven mechanisms from zero to high magnetic field.
AI.motivation: Optically readable molecular spins, especially photoexcited spin-triplet states in organic molecules, are promising room-temperature quantum sensors, but their utility depends on spin coherence (T2), which requires detailed mechanistic understanding.
AI.method: First-principles generalized cluster-correlation expansion (gCCE) simulations of Hahn-echo decoherence in pentacene guest molecules in a para-terphenyl host, systematically varying magnetic field and analyzing the roles of guest vs host molecules, specific nuclei, zero-field splitting (ZFS), and hyperfine parameters.
AI.result: Zero-field decoherence is dominated by ~6 guest nuclei, whereas high-field decoherence involves ~600 host nuclei; the longitudinal ZFS parameter D can prolong T2; and decoherence is governed by magnetic-field-dependent processes.
AI.conclusion: The findings clarify decoherence mechanisms in optically readable molecular spins, guiding synthetic enhancement and deployment as quantum probes.

title: Portable Vector NV-Diamond Magnetometer for Shot-Noise-Limited, Drift-Free Operation in Unshielded Environments
summary: Ensemble nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond magnetometers combine high sensitivity with vector-field reconstruction, but practical deployment is limited by errors arising from high-frequency laser noise during short-duration operations and slow-varying gain fluctuations and offset drift during long-term operation. Here, we present an integrated digital architecture for achieving NV magnetometry stability across distinct timescales. A dynamic differential readout continuously balances fluorescence and reference channels to suppress correlated laser noise. Second-derivative Lorentzian lineshape tracking enables in-situ correction of slope variations arising from slow changes in gain and optical excitation. We further identify temperature-induced bias-magnet fluctuations as a dominant source of long-term drift and introduce a magnetic eigenvector transformation that uses the intrinsic response of NV resonances to eliminate these variations. We show, under unshielded ambient conditions, that this architecture achieves an off-resonance noise factor of 1.0 $\pm$ 0.1, matching the fundamental limit with ten-fold suppression of long-term drift, enabling stable, field-ready quantum magnetometry.

AI.tldr: An integrated digital architecture enables ensemble NV-diamond magnetometry stability across timescales, achieving the fundamental noise limit (off-resonance noise factor 1.0 ± 0.1) with ten-fold long-term drift suppression under unshielded ambient conditions.
AI.motivation: Ensemble NV diamond magnetometers offer high sensitivity and vector-field reconstruction, but practical deployment is hindered by errors: high-frequency laser noise during short-duration operations, and slow-varying gain fluctuations plus offset drift during long-term operation. A unified approach addressing stability across distinct timescales is lacking.
AI.method: The work proposes an integrated digital architecture with three components: (1) a dynamic differential readout that continuously balances fluorescence and reference channels to suppress correlated laser noise; (2) second-derivative Lorentzian lineshape tracking for in-situ correction of slope variations from slow gain and optical-excitation changes; (3) identification of temperature-induced bias-magnet fluctuations as the dominant long-term drift source, addressed via a magnetic eigenvector transformation exploiting the intrinsic response of NV resonances.
AI.result: Under unshielded ambient conditions, the architecture achieves an off-resonance noise factor of 1.0 ± 0.1, matching the fundamental limit, together with ten-fold suppression of long-term drift.
AI.conclusion: The integrated digital architecture delivers stable, field-ready quantum magnetometry by reconciling short-timescale noise suppression and long-term drift correction within a single scheme.

title: Exact efficient simulation of noisy logical magic states using Clifford stabilizers
summary: The preparation of high-fidelity logical magic states is a crucial subroutine for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC). Predicting the performance of FTQC and developing improved protocols rely on numerical methods to classically simulate logical magic state preparation in the presence of noise. Clifford logic on Pauli-stabilizer codes with circuit-level Pauli errors can be efficiently simulated using Pauli-stabilizer formalism, but the non-Clifford operations required to prepare logical magic states render generic simulation inefficient. We introduce Clifford-stabilizer simulation, an exact and efficient algorithm based on updating a Clifford-stabilizer group to simulate noisy preparation protocols for a broad class of logical magic states used to implement non-Clifford gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy under circuit-level Pauli errors. Clifford-stabilizer simulation applies to a range of operations that commonly appear in preparation protocols for such logical magic states, including Pauli-stabilizer measurements, logical Clifford measurements, and transversal non-Clifford gates. Our algorithm for Clifford-stabilizer simulation maps a non-Clifford circuit with sampled circuit-level Pauli errors to a Clifford circuit that exactly reproduces its measurement outcome distribution, achieving time and space complexities polynomial in relevant protocol parameters. We perform exact simulation of magic state cultivation up to fault distance 7 by Clifford-stabilizer simulation. Our method provides a route to perform exact benchmarking of large-scale logical magic state preparation protocols required for useful FTQC.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Clifford-stabilizer simulation, an exact and efficient classical algorithm that simulates noisy preparation protocols for a broad class of logical magic states under circuit-level Pauli errors by mapping the non-Clifford circuit to an equivalent Clifford circuit with polynomial time and space complexity.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity logical magic state preparation is essential for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC). Predicting FTQC performance and developing improved protocols depend on classically simulating logical magic state preparation under noise. While Clifford logic on Pauli-stabilizer codes with circuit-level Pauli errors can be efficiently simulated via Pauli-stabilizer formalism, the non-Clifford operations needed to prepare logical magic states make generic simulation inefficient.
AI.method: The authors propose Clifford-stabilizer simulation, an exact and efficient algorithm that updates a Clifford-stabilizer group to simulate noisy preparation protocols for a broad class of logical magic states used to implement non-Clifford gates at the third level of the Clifford hierarchy under circuit-level Pauli errors. It supports common operations in such protocols, including Pauli-stabilizer measurements, logical Clifford measurements, and transversal non-Clifford gates. The algorithm maps a non-Clifford circuit with sampled circuit-level Pauli errors to a Clifford circuit that exactly reproduces its measurement outcome distribution, with time and space complexity polynomial in relevant protocol parameters.
AI.result: The authors perform exact simulation of magic state cultivation up to fault distance 7 using Clifford-stabilizer simulation.
AI.conclusion: Clifford-stabilizer simulation provides a route to exact benchmarking of large-scale logical magic state preparation protocols required for useful fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Classical Communication Protocol based on Joint Classical-Quantum Coding
summary: We introduce a robust quantum communication protocol that integrates classical error-control coding, entanglement distribution, and superdense coding. Classical error-correcting codes are used to mitigate dark counts and photon losses by determining the positions of qubit transmissions and protecting the data embedded through superdense coding. We derive conditions on the employed codes that guarantee successful error correction under a bounded error-frequency model. Moreover, upper bounds are derived on the performance of conventional superdense coding protected by classical error correction. It is shown that, under the same constraints on error frequency, suitable code configurations of the proposed protocol can exceed those upper bounds both in terms of data rate and energy efficiency. Finally, we develop a physical error model based on fiber attenuation, detector efficiency, dark counts, and time-slot duration, and use it to evaluate the effective performance of different configurations of error-correcting codes. The proposed approach is primarily suited for short-distance quantum links, as in Quantum Local Area Network (QLAN) where it can provide high communication throughput while integrating entanglement distribution directly into the communication process.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a robust quantum communication protocol combining classical error-control coding, entanglement distribution, and superdense coding to mitigate dark counts and photon losses, outperforming conventional error-corrected superdense coding in data rate and energy efficiency.
AI.motivation: Quantum communication suffers from dark counts and photon losses that degrade reliability. Conventional superdense coding protected only by classical error correction faces performance limits, motivating a more integrated protocol that jointly handles entanglement distribution and error mitigation.
AI.method: The protocol integrates classical error-correcting codes, entanglement distribution, and superdense coding. Classical codes determine qubit transmission positions and protect superdense-coded data. Conditions on codes are derived for guaranteed error correction under a bounded error-frequency model, and upper bounds on conventional error-corrected superdense coding are established. A physical error model based on fiber attenuation, detector efficiency, dark counts, and time-slot duration is developed to evaluate code configurations.
AI.result: Under identical error-frequency constraints, suitable code configurations of the proposed protocol exceed the upper bounds of conventional error-corrected superdense coding in both data rate and energy efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The approach is primarily suited for short-distance quantum links such as Quantum Local Area Networks (QLAN), providing high communication throughput while integrating entanglement distribution directly into the communication process.

title: Spin Grid States for Quantum Metrology in Atomic Clocks Limited by Spontaneous Emission
summary: Entanglement can enhance precision in phase estimation and in frequency estimation with atomic clocks, but it remains a central challenge to identify useful states and measurements under realistic noise processes. Here, we study quantum metrology with an ensemble of atoms subject to spontaneous emission, which limits frequency estimation by constraining the useful interrogation time. We identify spin grid states (SGSs) as the relevant near-optimal probes beyond a crossover at an ensemble size of 51, where GHZ-like states cease to be optimal. SGSs display a periodic grid on the Bloch sphere and can be generated with two one-axis-twisting (OAT) operations separated by a collective rotation. By optimizing the quantum Fisher information over permutationally symmetric states, we find that SGSs perform close to the globally optimal probes for intermediate and large ensembles, which turn out to be spin GKP states. We further present a sequential readout strategy that nearly saturates the corresponding quantum Fisher information. This strategy uses an OAT echo to map spontaneous-emission events onto collective rotations, making the corresponding jump sectors distinguishable and allowing the measurement basis to be conditioned on the number of decay events. Together, these results show that SGSs provide a practical route to quantum-enhanced phase and frequency metrology in atomic ensembles limited by spontaneous emission.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies spin grid states (SGSs) as near-optimal probes for quantum metrology with atomic ensembles under spontaneous emission, valid beyond a crossover ensemble size of 51 where GHZ-like states fail, and provides a sequential readout strategy that nearly saturates the quantum Fisher information.
AI.motivation: Entanglement can enhance precision in phase and frequency estimation with atomic clocks, but identifying useful states and measurements under realistic noise (specifically spontaneous emission) remains a central challenge. Spontaneous emission constrains the useful interrogation time, limiting frequency estimation.
AI.method: The authors optimize the quantum Fisher information over permutationally symmetric states to find optimal probes. They show SGSs can be generated with two one-axis-twisting (OAT) operations separated by a collective rotation. They also design a sequential readout strategy using an OAT echo to map spontaneous-emission events onto collective rotations, making jump sectors distinguishable and conditioning the measurement basis on the number of decay events.
AI.result: SGSs are identified as the relevant near-optimal probes beyond a crossover at an ensemble size of 51, where GHZ-like states cease to be optimal. SGSs perform close to the globally optimal probes (spin GKP states) for intermediate and large ensembles. The sequential readout strategy nearly saturates the corresponding quantum Fisher information.
AI.conclusion: SGSs provide a practical route to quantum-enhanced phase and frequency metrology in atomic ensembles limited by spontaneous emission.

title: Indistinguishability of single Raman photons from single atoms
summary: We theoretically investigate the indistinguishability of single photons generated from single trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions in a Raman scattering process driven by few-nanosecond excitation pulses. Of particular interest is how spontaneous decay back to the initial state affects Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) photon interference. Numerical simulations identify the mean number of back-decays as a measurable quantity that correlates with achievable HOM visibility. Optimization of the excitation pulse with respect to a trade-off between photon yield and indistinguishability is analyzed. Finally, we compare the performance of different trapped-ion species for long-range dual-rail entanglement swapping via HOM photon interference.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically studies single-photon indistinguishability from trapped 40Ca+ ions under few-nanosecond Raman excitation, linking back-decay events to Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility, optimizing the excitation pulse, and benchmarking ion species for long-range dual-rail entanglement swapping.
AI.motivation: Spontaneous decay back to the initial state during Raman single-photon generation degrades photon indistinguishability, which is critical for HOM interference and entanglement protocols; a quantitative understanding of this effect and of pulse trade-offs is needed.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations of single-photon emission from single trapped 40Ca+ ions driven by few-nanosecond Raman excitation pulses, quantifying back-decays and their correlation with HOM visibility, plus pulse optimization and comparison across trapped-ion species.
AI.result: The mean number of back-decays is identified as a measurable quantity correlating with achievable HOM visibility; a trade-off between photon yield and indistinguishability is characterized, and species-dependent performance for long-range dual-rail entanglement swapping via HOM interference is compared.
AI.conclusion: Back-decay statistics provide a practical metric for photon indistinguishability, and optimized Raman pulse parameters enable a balanced compromise between yield and visibility, informing ion-species choice for long-range entanglement swapping.

title: Strictly Localized Mixed States
summary: We study strictly localized mixed states in quantum field theory: states that are indistinguishable from vacuum outside some spacetime region. Such states are generated from the vacuum by so-called Licht maps. While the states associated with individual outcomes of local, projective measurements on the vacuum are not strictly localized, the corresponding non-selective states are strictly localized and even admit decompositions into strictly localized pure states. Remarkably, however, there are strictly localized mixed states that cannot be written as mixtures of pure states strictly localized to the same region. Such states can arise from unsharp local measurements. Finally, we extend Knight's theorem to mixed states, showing that strictly localized bosonic mixed states contain terms with arbitrarily high particle numbers.

AI.tldr: Strictly localized mixed states in QFT are generated by Licht maps; non-selective states from local projective measurements are strictly localized and decompose into strictly localized pure states, but some strictly localized mixed states (from unsharp measurements) cannot be written as mixtures of pure states localized to the same region, and strictly localized bosonic mixed states contain arbitrarily high particle numbers.
AI.motivation: To characterize strictly localized mixed states in quantum field theory—states indistinguishable from vacuum outside a spacetime region—and to clarify their structure, decomposition properties, and particle-number content.
AI.method: Analysis via Licht maps generating strictly localized states from vacuum; examination of local projective and unsharp local measurements; extension of Knight's theorem from pure to mixed states.
AI.result: Individual outcomes of local projective measurements on vacuum are not strictly localized, but non-selective states are and decompose into strictly localized pure states. Some strictly localized mixed states, arising from unsharp local measurements, cannot be decomposed as mixtures of pure states localized to the same region. Strictly localized bosonic mixed states contain terms with arbitrarily high particle numbers.
AI.conclusion: The class of strictly localized mixed states is richer than that of mixtures of strictly localized pure states, with unsharp measurements producing non-decomposable examples and bosonic cases exhibiting unbounded particle number.

title: Thermodynamic Uncertainty of Work in Time-Dependently Driven Open Quantum Systems
summary: We derive a thermodynamic uncertainty relation for work in an open quantum system driven by a time-dependent protocol and subject to repeated projective energy measurements. The protocol is represented by a sequence of protocol quenches separated by finite-time Lindblad evolution, so that work is accumulated at the quenches while dissipation occurs between them. The resulting work statistics obey the Gallavotti-Cohen symmetry to give rise to the Crooks and Jarzynski fluctuation relations. By perturbing the dissipative dynamics and combining the Cramér--Rao inequality with the quantum Fisher information, we obtain $\mathrm{Var}\,{\cal W}/[τ\partial_τ\langle{\cal W}\rangle]^2\ge 1/{\cal F}\ge\max(1/{\cal A},2/{\cal E})$, where $\langle{\cal W}\rangle$ is the work expectation value, $\mathrm{Var}\,{\cal W}$ is the variance of work, ${\cal F}$ is the Fisher information, ${\cal A}$ is the dynamical activity, ${\cal E}$ is the dimensionless entropy production, and $τ$ is the switching time interval between quenches. The two thermodynamic bounds follow from two independent perturbations that generate the same response of the work statistics. We illustrate the relation for a dissipative two-level system under square-wave and sinusoidal driving and show that the tighter thermodynamic bound can depend on the driving protocol and switching time scale.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a thermodynamic uncertainty relation for work in an open quantum system driven by a time-dependent protocol with repeated projective energy measurements, linking work fluctuations to dynamical activity and entropy production via quantum Fisher information.
AI.motivation: Thermodynamic uncertainty relations constrain fluctuations of thermodynamic quantities by dissipation, but extending these relations to work statistics in open quantum systems under driven protocols with measurements remains an open problem. The authors aim to derive such a relation combining fluctuation relations, quantum Fisher information, and thermodynamic bounds.
AI.method: The protocol is modeled as a sequence of quenches separated by finite-time Lindblad evolution, where work accumulates at quenches and dissipation occurs between them. The work statistics are shown to obey Gallavotti-Cohen symmetry, yielding Crooks and Jarzynski fluctuation relations. By perturbing the dissipative dynamics and combining the Cramér-Rao inequality with quantum Fisher information, the authors derive bounds involving dynamical activity and dimensionless entropy production.
AI.result: The derived relation is Var W / [τ ∂_τ ⟨W⟩]^2 ≥ 1/F ≥ max(1/A, 2/E), where ⟨W⟩ is the work expectation, Var W the work variance, F the Fisher information, A the dynamical activity, E the dimensionless entropy production, and τ the switching time interval. The two bounds arise from two independent perturbations generating the same work-statistics response. For a dissipative two-level system under square-wave and sinusoidal driving, the tighter bound depends on both the driving protocol and switching time scale.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that thermodynamic uncertainty relations for work can be established in open quantum systems with repeated energy measurements, with the tighter of the dynamical activity and entropy production bounds depending on the specific driving protocol and time scale. This connects fluctuation relations, quantum metrology tools, and thermodynamic bounds in a unified framework.

title: Eigenstate thermalization beyond the envelope: exact two-point overlap statistics in random free fermions
summary:
Eigenstate thermalization constrains the smooth dependence of observables on energy, but it does not by itself fix the microscopic statistics of the overlaps between many-body eigenstates and a chosen basis: the smooth envelope is a one-point statement, and the fluctuation field it leaves undetermined carries a structured two-point covariance. We establish this distinction, and solve that fluctuation field exactly, in random free fermions---an ensemble of Slater-determinant eigenstates built from a Gaussian orthogonal single-particle Hamiltonian, whose eigenstate thermalization was established by Magán.
  In this ensemble every channel overlap is a minor of a Haar-distributed orthogonal matrix, so its statistics follow from classical random-matrix theory. The one-point law is exactly flat for every channel, with an exact moment hierarchy that is not Porter--Thomas: small intensities are enhanced algebraically rather than by the exponential Porter--Thomas form, and the mean sector carries a negative, order-one correlation correction of purely normalization origin. The two-point covariance closes exactly at the Gaussian fixed point: it is organized by the number of one-body modes shared by two eigenstates and by the number of modes shared by two channels, and its energy-resolved form factorizes into this geometry times the classical convolution of the single-particle semicircle, from which the two-resolvent covariance follows by an integral transform. Exact finite-size computations confirm all closed forms, and the structural identities of the dictionary hold at machine precision. The results provide an exactly solvable microscopic realization of the two-point fluctuation sector underlying multi-resolvent descriptions of eigenstate thermalization: a smooth envelope does not determine fine-grained fluctuations.

AI.tldr: The paper distinguishes the smooth energy envelope of eigenstate thermalization from its fluctuation field and exactly solves the two-point covariance of basis overlaps for random free fermions, showing the one-point statistics are flat (non-Porter-Thomas) and the two-point covariance closes at a Gaussian fixed point.
AI.motivation: Eigenstate thermalization fixes only the smooth, one-point energy dependence of observables, leaving the fine-grained fluctuation field undetermined. The authors argue the undetermined fluctuations carry a structured two-point covariance, so a smooth envelope alone cannot fix microscopic overlap statistics, and they seek an exactly solvable model where this fluctuation sector can be solved.
AI.method: They study random free fermions: Slater-determinant eigenstates built from a Gaussian orthogonal single-particle Hamiltonian, where eigenstate thermalization was previously established. Each channel overlap is a minor of a Haar-distributed orthogonal matrix, so its statistics are derived from classical random-matrix theory via minors, moment hierarchies, two-point covariance organized by shared one-body and channel modes, energy-resolved form factors, semicircle convolutions, and an integral transform to the two-resolvent covariance, verified by exact finite-size computations.
AI.result: The one-point law is exactly flat for every channel with a non-Porter-Thomas moment hierarchy: small intensities are algebraically enhanced rather than exponentially suppressed, and the mean sector has a negative order-one correlation correction of normalization origin. The two-point covariance closes exactly at the Gaussian fixed point, organized by shared one-body modes between eigenstates and shared modes between channels; its energy-resolved form factor factorizes into this geometry times a convolution of the single-particle semicircle. Exact finite-size computations confirm all closed forms, and structural dictionary identities hold at machine precision.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an exactly solvable microscopic realization of the two-point fluctuation sector underlying multi-resolvent descriptions of eigenstate thermalization, demonstrating that a smooth envelope does not determine fine-grained fluctuations.

title: Constant sized support state distillation with qubit recycling
summary: In order to circumvent that no universal set of gates can be achieved on a given quantum error-correcting codes, additional gates can be performed through magic state injection. This however requires to have access to high fidelity magic state, which can be obtained by the distillation of low quality states to fewer higher quality ones. In this paper, we provide a family of distillation protocols able to produce diagonal states at every level of the Clifford hierarchy. This family is obtained recursively using code doubling techniques and leveraging qubit recycling, the fact that some idle qubits of the protocols can be measured and re-used. At a given level of the Clifford hierarchy, we show that the protocols we derive can be performed at arbitrary high distance on a fix number of logical qubits. This family recovers many known efficient protocols, and uncovers new ones, such as a $111 \to 1$ protocol for $|T\rangle$ state distillation at distance $7$, which are the most compact in term of volume. Finally, we discuss possible extension of this framework for distillation protocols producing more than one output state.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a recursive family of magic state distillation protocols based on code doubling and qubit recycling, capable of producing diagonal states at every level of the Clifford hierarchy, with arbitrarily high distance on a fixed number of logical qubits.
AI.motivation: Universal quantum computation cannot be achieved with transversal gates alone on a given quantum error-correcting code, necessitating magic state injection, which requires high-fidelity magic states obtained by distilling low-quality states into fewer higher-quality ones. Existing distillation protocols are limited, motivating a unified framework to systematically generate efficient protocols across the Clifford hierarchy.
AI.method: The authors construct distillation protocols recursively using code doubling techniques and exploit qubit recycling, where idle qubits in the protocols are measured and reused. This yields a family of protocols producing diagonal states at every level of the Clifford hierarchy.
AI.result: The derived protocols can operate at arbitrary high distance on a fixed number of logical qubits at any given Clifford hierarchy level. The family recovers many known efficient protocols and reveals new ones, notably a 111→1 protocol for |T⟩ state distillation at distance 7, which is the most compact in terms of volume.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a systematic, recursive approach to designing efficient magic state distillation protocols across the Clifford hierarchy, and the authors discuss possible extensions for protocols producing more than one output state.

title: Probabilistic Error Cancellation for Single-Mode Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Codes
summary: In order to solve practical problems on a quantum computer, it is necessary to use fault-tolerant quantum error correction schemes to overcome noise: the errors arising from imperfections in physical components. The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code aims at achieving this in a hardware efficient manner by encoding finite-dimensional logical subspaces in the Hilbert space of one or more continuous variable modes. In near term implementations, however, it is not feasible to eliminate errors entirely, so it is natural to also employ alternative error mitigation techniques together with error correction. In this work, we study a quantum error mitigation method known as probabilistic error cancellation in the context of the GKP code. We compare Steane-type and teleportation-based GKP error correction, and calculate the sampling overheads associated with the technique for square and hexagonal GKP codes. We employ the stabilizer subsystem decomposition for GKP codes to obtain an effective logical channel for noisy operations that is used to express the ideal one of a target logical unitary. We consider noise from finite squeezing on the data and the two ancilla modes, needed for error correction, and examine the relationship between the sampling overhead and the noise for different decoding methods.
