Our results are calculated for single- and two-qubit GKP Clifford gates and one round of error correction, and show the nontrivial combination of error correction and mitigation in continuous variable codes.

AI.tldr: This work applies probabilistic error cancellation (PEM) to Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) error correction, comparing Steane-type and teleportation-based correction for square and hexagonal codes. Using the stabilizer subsystem decomposition to derive effective logical channels under finite-squeezing noise, it computes sampling overheads for single- and two-qubit Clifford gates and examines how overhead depends on noise and decoding method.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum error correction is required for practical quantum computation, and GKP codes provide hardware-efficient encoding of finite-dimensional logical subspaces in continuous variable modes. However, in near-term implementations errors cannot be fully eliminated, motivating the combination of error correction with error mitigation techniques. The motivation is to study how probabilistic error cancellation behaves in the GKP setting and how it interacts with error correction.
AI.method: The authors study probabilistic error cancellation in the context of the GKP code. They compare Steane-type and teleportation-based GKP error correction and compute the associated sampling overheads for square and hexagonal GKP codes. They employ the stabilizer subsystem decomposition for GKP codes to obtain an effective logical channel for noisy operations, which is used to express the ideal target logical unitary. Noise from finite squeezing on the data mode and the two ancilla modes required for error correction is considered, and the relationship between sampling overhead and noise is examined for different decoding methods.
AI.result: Sampling overheads are calculated for single- and two-qubit GKP Clifford gates and one round of error correction, for square and hexagonal GKP codes and for both Steane-type and teleportation-based error correction. The results show the nontrivial combination of error correction and mitigation in continuous variable codes, with overhead depending on the noise level and the chosen decoding method.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that probabilistic error cancellation can be integrated with GKP error correction, revealing a nontrivial interplay between error correction and mitigation in continuous variable codes. The sampling overhead for the mitigation technique depends on both the noise (finite squeezing) and the decoding method, highlighting the importance of jointly designing correction and mitigation strategies for near-term GKP implementations.

title: Large-scale NMR simulation on a trapped-ion quantum computer
summary: Simulating nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra is a promising application of quantum simulation. Using Quantinuum's System Model H2, a trapped-ion quantum computer, we demonstrate an end-to-end, large-scale digital NMR simulation of a classically challenging benchmark molecule, 1,2-di-tert-butyl-diphosphane. We implement a hardware-efficient reduction of the nuclear-spin Hamiltonian, enabling Trotterized real-time evolution of an effective 21-spin model with tailored error suppression to reduce the effects of device noise. The reconstructed liquid-state proton NMR spectrum agrees with classical reference calculations and reproduces key spectroscopic features that previous quantum hardware demonstrations did not capture. Given the widespread use of NMR in chemical analysis and industrial research, these results advance digital quantum simulation of NMR spectra towards practical quantum utility.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates an end-to-end, large-scale digital NMR simulation of a classically challenging molecule (1,2-di-tert-butyl-diphosphane) on a trapped-ion quantum computer (Quantinuum H2), implementing a hardware-efficient Hamiltonian reduction for an effective 21-spin model with tailored error suppression.
AI.motivation: NMR spectrum simulation is a promising application of quantum simulation. Prior quantum hardware demonstrations failed to reproduce key spectroscopic features, so a larger-scale simulation is needed to advance digital NMR simulation toward practical quantum utility.
AI.method: Uses Quantinuum's System Model H2 trapped-ion quantum computer for a digital NMR simulation. Implements a hardware-efficient reduction of the nuclear-spin Hamiltonian, enabling Trotterized real-time evolution of an effective 21-spin model, with tailored error suppression to reduce device noise.
AI.result: The reconstructed liquid-state proton NMR spectrum agrees with classical reference calculations and reproduces key spectroscopic features that previous quantum hardware demonstrations did not capture.
AI.conclusion: Given the widespread use of NMR in chemical analysis and industrial research, these results advance digital quantum simulation of NMR spectra towards practical quantum utility.

title: Thouless pumping via discrete jumping of the adiabatic Hamiltonian
summary: Thouless pumping is a celebrated topological effect that enables quantized particle transport and holds promise for applications in quantum technologies. However, the standard adiabatic pumping theory dictate that the Hamiltonian must be varied continuously and slowly throughout the whole pumping process. In this work, we show that Thouless pumping can be realized by using only discrete sampling of the Hamiltonian, removing the conventional constraint of continuous and slow change of control. Specifically, we select particular parameter points of the Hamiltonian for conventional continuous quantum adiabatic evolution, and then apply the Hamiltonian at these parameter points which induces a geodesic evolution for the pseudospin with a given quasimomentum. This realizes an adiabatic evolution for the Thouless pumping according to a necessary and sufficient condition for quantum adiabatic evolution.

AI.tldr: This work demonstrates that Thouless pumping can be realized using only discrete sampling of the Hamiltonian, eliminating the conventional requirement for continuous and slow parameter variation.
AI.motivation: Standard adiabatic pumping theory requires the Hamiltonian to be varied continuously and slowly throughout the entire pumping process, which imposes a stringent control constraint. This work aims to remove this constraint.
AI.method: The authors select particular parameter points of the Hamiltonian corresponding to conventional continuous quantum adiabatic evolution, and then apply the Hamiltonian at these discrete parameter points, inducing a geodesic evolution for the pseudospin at a given quasimomentum. This achieves adiabatic evolution for Thouless pumping based on a necessary and sufficient condition for quantum adiabatic evolution.
AI.result: Thouless pumping is realized through discrete sampling of the Hamiltonian rather than continuous, slow parameter variation.
AI.conclusion: Thouless pumping can be achieved without the conventional constraint of continuous and slow control change, broadening the conditions under which this topological effect can be implemented.

title: Floquet Theory and Average Hamiltonian Theory Revisited: Equivalence, Convergence and Applications to NMR
summary:
An accurate theoretical treatment of periodically driven quantum systems is crucial for various fields in the exact sciences, for instance Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Conventionally, either average Hamiltonian theory or Floquet theory is used to predict or describe experimental outcomes, such as the time evolution or the spectra yielding the information of the sample under study. A detailed analysis of the equivalence of these two approaches with an emphasis on applications in NMR will help to improve the theoretical understanding of NMR experiments.
  In this work, we identify the Floquet-Magnus expansion as essential to prove the mathematical equivalence of Floquet theory and average Hamiltonian theory. We advocate a calculation scheme which is less prone to algebraic mistakes because explicit integration is avoided. On this basis, we provide the first four orders of both theories. We further examine their applicability to some experiments in NMR. As examples, we investigate the Bloch-Siegert shift and dipolar coupled spin systems under magic-angle spinning.
  Based on our analysis, we recommend the use of the Floquet-Van Vleck approach including both the effective Hamiltonian and the kick operator. The consistent separation of secular and non-secular contributions appears to be especially advantageous for numerical robustness. Its accuracy is about three times better than the one provided by average Hamiltonian theory despite their formal equivalence.
  Our findings provide important insights into the theoretical background of Floquet theory and average Hamiltonian theory. This includes the extent of their algebraic and perturbative equivalence, with an emphasis on how these findings are of relevance in the analysis of solid-state NMR experiments.

AI.tldr: This work proves the mathematical equivalence of Floquet theory and average Hamiltonian theory via the Floquet-Magnus expansion, provides the first four orders of both, and recommends the Floquet-Van Vleck approach (effective Hamiltonian plus kick operator) for NMR applications due to superior numerical robustness and ~3x better accuracy.
AI.motivation: An accurate theoretical treatment of periodically driven quantum systems is crucial in fields such as NMR spectroscopy. Conventionally, either average Hamiltonian theory (AHT) or Floquet theory is used to predict or describe experimental outcomes (time evolution, spectra). A detailed analysis of the equivalence of these two approaches, with emphasis on NMR applications, would improve theoretical understanding of NMR experiments.
AI.method: The authors identify the Floquet-Magnus expansion as essential to prove the mathematical equivalence of Floquet theory and average Hamiltonian theory. They advocate a calculation scheme that avoids explicit integration, reducing susceptibility to algebraic mistakes, and derive the first four orders of both theories. They then examine applicability to NMR experiments, investigating the Bloch-Siegert shift and dipolar coupled spin systems under magic-angle spinning.
AI.result: The analysis yields the first four orders of both theories and demonstrates their algebraic and perturbative equivalence. Examining the Bloch-Siegert shift and dipolar coupled spins under magic-angle spinning, the authors find the Floquet-Van Vleck approach—including both the effective Hamiltonian and the kick operator—to be preferable: consistent separation of secular and non-secular contributions improves numerical robustness, and its accuracy is approximately three times better than that of average Hamiltonian theory despite formal equivalence.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide important insights into the theoretical background of Floquet theory and average Hamiltonian theory, clarifying the extent of their algebraic and perturbative equivalence and highlighting their relevance to the analysis of solid-state NMR experiments. The authors recommend the Floquet-Van Vleck approach with both effective Hamiltonian and kick operator for practical use.

title: Phase-stable voltage bias for Josephson photonics devices
summary: Parametric interactions are foundational to superconducting quantum technologies, yet conventional microwave-driven pumping introduces parasitic Kerr nonlinearities and higher-order harmonics that limit device performance. Josephson Photonics (JP) avoids these parasitics by utilizing dc-biased junctions but has remained constrained by high phase noise and the absence of a stable phase reference. Here, we overcome this limitation by integrating a Josephson voltage standard (JVS) to establish a noise-tolerant phase reference, and demonstrate that this reference is coherently transferred to an inelastic Cooper-pair tunneling amplifier (ICTA) via the superconducting order parameter.The resulting low-phase-noise architecture yields a 14-dB enhancement in averaged gain and better quantum-limited noise performance. Critically, the phase reference enables the first observation of phase-sensitive gain and sqeezing in a dc-biased amplifier. By reconciling clean, Kerr-free nonlinearities with phase-coherent drive, our architecture establishes a robust platform for high-purity parametric processes in superconducting circuits.

AI.tldr: By integrating a Josephson voltage standard (JVS) as a noise-tolerant phase reference and transferring it coherently to an inelastic Cooper-pair tunneling amplifier (ICTA), the authors achieve a 14-dB gain enhancement, near quantum-limited noise, and the first phase-sensitive gain and squeezing in a dc-biased amplifier.
AI.motivation: Conventional microwave-driven parametric pumping in superconducting quantum technologies introduces parasitic Kerr nonlinearities and higher-order harmonics that degrade device performance. Josephson Photonics (JP) avoids these parasitics using dc-biased junctions, but it has been limited by high phase noise and the lack of a stable phase reference.
AI.method: The authors integrate a Josephson voltage standard (JVS) to establish a noise-tolerant phase reference and demonstrate that this reference is coherently transferred to an inelastic Cooper-pair tunneling amplifier (ICTA) via the superconducting order parameter.
AI.result: The low-phase-noise architecture yields a 14-dB enhancement in averaged gain and improved quantum-limited noise performance. Critically, the phase reference enables the first observation of phase-sensitive gain and squeezing in a dc-biased amplifier.
AI.conclusion: By reconciling clean, Kerr-free nonlinearities with phase-coherent drive, the proposed architecture establishes a robust platform for high-purity parametric processes in superconducting circuits.

title: Preparation-protocol-dependent quantum Mpemba dynamics in a magnetically tunable graphene nanotorus qubit
summary: We investigate the quantum Mpemba effect in a graphene nanotorus qubit and show that its strength depends strongly on how the initial state is prepared. We compare two protocols that share the same final Hamiltonian, thermal bath, and Markovian Liouvillian: bare Gibbs preparation, in which the coherent drive is switched on only at the final quench, and driven steady-state preparation, in which the initial states are stationary states of the driven dynamics. Using the distance to the final stationary state and an integrated Mpemba parameter, we find broad regions of strong anomalous relaxation for bare Gibbs preparation, with $M_B$ approaching unity, whereas the driven steady-state protocol almost completely suppresses the effect. A Liouvillian-mode analysis reveals the mechanism: the bare Gibbs protocol typically yields a smaller hot-state weight in the slow active sector than the cold state, $R_s<1$, while the driven steady-state protocol predominantly gives $R_s>1$. Since the final Liouvillian spectrum is identical for both protocols at corresponding parameter points, the contrast originates from preparation-dependent modal weights rather than from changes in the decay-rate hierarchy. These results identify state preparation as a control parameter for anomalous quantum relaxation in a curved graphene qubit.

AI.tldr: The quantum Mpemba effect (QME) in a graphene nanotorus qubit is shown to be controlled by state preparation: a bare Gibbs preparation produces strong anomalous relaxation (Mpemba parameter approaching unity), while a driven steady-state preparation with the same final Hamiltonian, bath, and Liouvillian almost fully suppresses it.
AI.motivation: The QME—where a hotter state relaxes faster than a colder one—has been studied in various platforms, but how the preparation protocol shapes its strength in a curved graphene qubit remains unclear. The authors aim to identify state preparation as a control knob for anomalous quantum relaxation.
AI.method: Two protocols sharing identical final Hamiltonian, thermal bath, and Markovian Liouvillian are compared: (i) bare Gibbs preparation, where the coherent drive is switched on only at the final quench, and (ii) driven steady-state preparation, where initial states are stationary states of the driven dynamics. The analysis uses the distance to the final stationary state and an integrated Mpemba parameter, complemented by a Liouvillian-mode decomposition.
AI.result: Bare Gibbs preparation yields broad regions of strong anomalous relaxation with the Mpemba parameter $M_B$ approaching unity, whereas the driven steady-state protocol almost completely suppresses the effect. Liouvillian-mode analysis shows the bare Gibbs protocol typically gives a smaller hot-state weight in the slow active sector than the cold state ($R_s<1$), while the driven steady-state protocol predominantly gives $R_s>1$.
AI.conclusion: Because the final Liouvillian spectrum is identical for both protocols at corresponding parameter points, the observed contrast stems from preparation-dependent modal weights rather than from changes in the decay-rate hierarchy. State preparation thus acts as a control parameter for anomalous quantum relaxation in a curved graphene qubit.

title: Real-Space Renormalization of Stabilizer Rényi Entropies in Spin Chains
summary: Stabilizer states constitute an important class of quantum states that can be generated from computational-basis states using Pauli operators and Clifford gates. Although they may exhibit substantial multipartite entanglement, quantum circuits restricted to stabilizer operations can be efficiently simulated classically and therefore cannot, by themselves, provide a quantum computational advantage. Such an advantage requires non-stabilizer resources, commonly referred to as quantum magic. In this paper, we investigate the non-stabilizerness of quantum states arising in a class of spin Hamiltonians by computing their stabilizer Rényi entropies. Using real-space renormalization-group techniques, we obtain a closed-form expression valid in the low-energy, large-distance regime. We analyze how quantum magic evolves under coarse-graining and explore its behavior across different parameter regimes and quantum phases.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies the "quantum magic" (non-stabilizerness) of spin Hamiltonian ground states via stabilizer Rényi entropies, deriving a closed-form low-energy expression using real-space renormalization-group methods and tracking magic under coarse-graining across quantum phases.
AI.motivation: Stabilizer states are classically efficiently simulable, so they offer no quantum computational advantage. That advantage requires non-stabilizer resources ("quantum magic"). Understanding how magic arises and behaves in physical many-body states, and how it relates to quantum phases, is therefore important but not well characterized.
AI.method: The authors compute stabilizer Rényi entropies as measures of non-stabilizerness for quantum states emerging in a class of spin Hamiltonians, employing real-space renormalization-group techniques to obtain a closed-form expression valid in the low-energy, large-distance regime.
AI.result: A closed-form expression for the stabilizer Rényi entropy is derived in the low-energy, large-distance regime. The evolution of quantum magic under coarse-graining is analyzed, along with its behavior across different parameter regimes and quantum phases.
AI.conclusion: Quantum magic in spin Hamiltonians can be characterized analytically through stabilizer Rényi entropies in the low-energy limit, and its scaling and coarse-graining behavior reveals how non-stabilizerness varies across parameter regimes and quantum phases.

title: Geometric quantifier of the incompatibility of single-particle property attribution in indistinguishable boson systems
summary: Entanglement in indistinguishable particle systems can be characterized by the impossibility of unambiguously attributing a complete set of physical properties to the individual constituent particles. In this work, we introduce a geometric quantifier of the incompatibility of such simultaneous property attribution for pure states of $N$ indistinguishable bosons. Using the Majorana stellar representation, any symmetric multi-qubit state can be expressed as the symmetrization of constituent single-particle states, allowing the associated single-particle properties to be directly linked with the corresponding Majorana stars. This establishes a direct connection between the geometry of the Majorana representation on the Bloch sphere and the entanglement criterion based on the attribution of single-particle properties in systems of identical two-level bosons. We then generalize this geometric approach to higher-dimensional bosons, extending the quantifier from qubits to qudits, while retaining a geometric interpretation of property-attribution incompatibility in terms of Fubini-Study angles.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a geometric quantifier of entanglement for pure states of N indistinguishable bosons, based on the incompatibility of simultaneously attributing a complete set of physical properties to individual particles, using the Majorana stellar representation.
AI.motivation: Entanglement in indistinguishable particle systems is characterized by the impossibility of unambiguously attributing a complete set of physical properties to individual constituent particles. A geometric quantifier for this property-attribution incompatibility is needed, but existing approaches lack a direct geometric connection, especially for higher-dimensional bosons.
AI.method: Using the Majorana stellar representation, any symmetric multi-qubit state is expressed as the symmetrization of constituent single-particle states, linking single-particle properties to the Majorana stars. This connects the geometry of the Majorana representation on the Bloch sphere with the entanglement criterion based on single-particle property attribution. The approach is then generalized from qubits to qudits, retaining a geometric interpretation via Fubini-Study angles.
AI.result: A direct connection is established between the geometry of the Majorana representation on the Bloch sphere and the entanglement criterion based on single-particle property attribution for identical two-level bosons. The quantifier is extended from qubits to qudits while preserving a geometric interpretation of property-attribution incompatibility.
AI.conclusion: The geometric quantifier provides a unified framework for characterizing entanglement in indistinguishable bosonic systems via the incompatibility of simultaneous property attribution, generalizable from qubits to qudits through a Fubini-Study angle interpretation.

title: ConteXtuAlity: an open source Python package for contextuality
summary: We present an open source Python package, ConteXtuAlity, for computing various quantities related to contextuality. This package features an interface to the sheaf-theoretic framework for contextuality, providing an implementation of measurement scenarios and empirical models as well as linear programs to compute the contextual fraction and the signalling fraction. In this work, we demonstrate the package's features and give examples of its use. We also provide benchmarks, demonstrating how performances scale with the size of measurement scenarios. The package is designed for both experienced theorists and newcomers to the field of contextuality alike, with an emphasis on flexibility and extensibility.

AI.tldr: The authors present "ConteXtuAlity," an open-source Python package for computing contextuality-related quantities, interfaced with the sheaf-theoretic framework and offering tools for measurement scenarios, empirical models, and linear programs for contextual and signalling fractions.
AI.motivation: Contextuality is a central concept in quantum foundations and quantum information, but computing contextuality-related quantities requires specialized formal machinery. There is a need for accessible, flexible, and extensible software that lowers the barrier for both experienced theorists and newcomers.
AI.method: The package provides an interface to the sheaf-theoretic framework for contextuality. It implements measurement scenarios and empirical models, along with linear programs to compute the contextual fraction and the signalling fraction. The work demonstrates the package's features, gives usage examples, and provides benchmarks showing how performance scales with measurement scenario size.
AI.result: The package is demonstrated through examples of its use, and benchmarks quantify how its performance scales with the size of measurement scenarios.
AI.conclusion: ConteXtuAlity is an open-source, flexible, and extensible Python package aimed at both experienced theorists and newcomers to contextuality, with an emphasis on ease of use and extensibility.

title: Forbidden Subspaces in Quantum State Smoothing
summary: A system between a preparation and a post-selection has had no agreed state since 1964. With positivity as the criterion, a post-selection admits an interval of orderings around the symmetric one exactly when the subspace it forbids is spanned by eigenvectors of a full-rank filtered state. Otherwise it certifies contextuality, testable on a qubit. The averaged filtered state carries the entanglement spectrum of the record, so the smallest forbidden subspaces a symmetry allows are even-dimensional in the Haldane class and odd in the trivial one. That parity is the record's topological class.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the long-standing ambiguity of assigning a state to a system between preparation and post-selection. Using positivity as the criterion, it shows that a post-selection admits a range of orderings around the symmetric one precisely when its forbidden subspace is spanned by eigenvectors of a full-rank filtered state; otherwise it certifies contextuality, testable on a qubit. The parity of the smallest symmetry-allowed forbidden subspace encodes the record's topological class.
AI.motivation: Since 1964 there has been no agreed way to define the state of a system between preparation and post-selection. The paper aims to settle this ambiguity by grounding the assignment in positivity, and to connect the resulting structure to contextuality and topology.
AI.method: Positivity is used as the defining criterion for admissible states. The authors analyze the subspace a post-selection forbids and ask when it is spanned by eigenvectors of a full-rank filtered state, yielding an interval of orderings around the symmetric ordering. When this fails, contextuality is diagnosed and tested on a qubit. The averaged filtered state is shown to carry the entanglement spectrum of the record, allowing a parity analysis of the smallest allowed forbidden subspaces under a symmetry.
AI.result: A post-selection admits an interval of orderings around the symmetric one exactly when its forbidden subspace is spanned by eigenvectors of a full-rank filtered state; otherwise it certifies contextuality, testable on a qubit. The smallest forbidden subspaces a symmetry allows are even-dimensional in the Haldane class and odd-dimensional in the trivial class, and this parity is identified as the record's topological class.
AI.conclusion: Positivity provides a principled basis for defining states between preparation and post-selection, and the parity of the smallest symmetry-allowed forbidden subspace serves as a topological invariant of the record.

title: Generalised quantum Stein's lemma more robust than ever
summary: The generalised quantum Stein's lemma is a key result in quantum hypothesis testing, and connects this fundamental primitive of quantum information processing with quantum resource manipulation, a task that is central for technological applications. Prior works have proved this statement in the idealised setting of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sequences of quantum states, and recent extensions consider also sources that are 'close' to i.i.d., according to the strict notion put forth by Mazzola, Sutter, and Renner. For several applications, however, one would need to consider yet more general sources. We establish a version of the generalised quantum Stein's lemma that is conceptually much simpler and general, as it applies to any source that is asymptotically close to an i.i.d. state with respect to the normalised quantum Wasserstein distance of order 1. As an immediate consequence, we solve the Stein exponent of a scenario where the null hypothesis is arbitrarily varying, expressing it in terms of i.i.d. Stein exponents corresponding to arbitrary states in the convex hull of the null hypothesis base set.

AI.motivation: The generalised quantum Stein's lemma links quantum hypothesis testing to quantum resource manipulation, a central primitive for technological applications. Prior proofs only covered i.i.d. sequences or sources merely "close" to i.i.d. in the strict sense of Mazzola, Sutter, and Renner, while many applications require more general sources.
AI.method: The authors derive a conceptually simpler and more general version of the generalised quantum Stein's lemma that applies to any source asymptotically close to an i.i.d. state with respect to the normalised quantum Wasserstein distance of order 1.
AI.result: The generalised lemma is proved under this weaker and more broadly applicable closeness condition. As an immediate consequence, the Stein exponent is solved for a scenario where the null hypothesis is arbitrarily varying, expressed via i.i.d. Stein exponents corresponding to arbitrary states in the convex hull of the null hypothesis base set.
AI.conclusion: The work substantially generalises the generalised quantum Stein's lemma by relaxing the required similarity to i.i.d. sources, and yields a solution to the Stein exponent for arbitrarily varying null hypotheses.

title: Optimal Linear-Rate Conversion of Unknown Mixed Qubit States via SWAP Tests
comment: 5 pages main body + appendices; 1 table and 1 figure; comments welcome!
summary: By consuming multiple copies of an unknown qubit state, one can modify its purity while preserving the direction of its Bloch vector. We determine the maximum linear rate at which qubit states of different purities can be interconverted, allowing a nonzero error, quantified, for instance, by the trace distance, provided that it vanishes in the limit of infinitely many copies. Interestingly, the optimal conversion rate is determined by the two eigenvalues of the complex right-logarithmic-derivative (RLD) Fisher information matrix associated with $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ rotations of the qubit state. When the output qubits have higher purity, corresponding to concentration, the optimal rate is given by the ratio of the maximum eigenvalues of the input and output RLD matrices. In contrast, when the output qubits have lower purity, corresponding to dilution, the optimal rate is given by the ratio of their minimum eigenvalues. Remarkably, both concentration and dilution can be implemented using SWAP tests as the only nontrivial two-qubit measurement primitive, together with ancillary qubits initially prepared in maximally mixed states, without requiring any additional two-qubit gates. Our work thus provides a novel operational interpretation of the full complex RLD Fisher information matrix. Crucially, its antisymmetric, purely imaginary part encodes geometric information beyond the statistical distance between density operators and plays an essential role in determining the optimal state-conversion rates.

AI.tldr: The paper determines the maximum linear rate for interconverting qubit states of different purities (while preserving the Bloch-vector direction), allowing asymptotically vanishing error. The optimal rates are set by the eigenvalues of the complex RLD Fisher information matrix, and both concentration and dilution can be realized using only SWAP tests plus maximally mixed ancillas.
AI.motivation: Consuming many copies of an unknown qubit lets one change its purity while keeping the Bloch-vector direction, but the fundamental limits on such purity interconversion—and what physical quantity governs them—were unclear. The work seeks to characterize optimal conversion rates and provide an operational interpretation of the full complex RLD Fisher information matrix, including its usually neglected antisymmetric imaginary part.

They relate the achievable rates to the eigenvalues of the complex right-logarithmic-derivative (RLD) Fisher information matrix associated with SU(2) rotations of the qubit, analyzing concentration (purity increase) and dilution (purity decrease) separately. They also give explicit protocols using SWAP tests as the only nontrivial two-qubit measurement and ancillas in maximally mixed states, with no extra two-qubit gates.

For concentration (higher output purity), the optimal rate equals the ratio of the maximum eigenvalues of the output and input RLD matrices; for dilution (lower output purity), it equals the ratio of their minimum eigenvalues. Both concentration and dilution are implementable using only SWAP tests and maximally mixed ancillas, requiring no additional two-qubit gates.

In particular, its antisymmetric, purely imaginary part encodes geometric information beyond the statistical distance between density operators and plays an essential role in determining optimal state-conversion rates.

title: Exceptional Topology Survives Strong Hermitian Fields in Radiative Atomic Arrays
comment: 4 figures in the main paper, with supplementary materials
summary: Exceptional points are topological defects of complex band structures that are stable against weak perturbations, yet in bounded two-band systems they are ultimately removed by a sufficiently strong Hermitian field. Here we demonstrate a striking exception in a two-dimensional subwavelength atomic array. Along a continuous square-to-triangular deformation at fixed magnetic field, the bulk passes between line-gapped topological regions with band Chern numbers (C_1,C_2)=(2,-2) through a gapless exceptional region. Within a finite interval of lattice deformation, increasing the magnetic field merely drives the exceptional points toward the light cone because of the singular radiative dipolar couplings. We further show that skin localization toward open boundaries responds non-monotonically to the same field. An intermediate field drives a bipolar skin localization, with bulk modes accumulating at opposite edges, whereas stronger fields suppress boundary localization. Our results establish the interplay of lattice geometry, light-cone singularity, and Hermitian magnetic field as a route to engineering Chern and exceptional topology beyond the conventional strong-field limit.

AI.tldr: In a 2D subwavelength atomic array, a square-to-triangular deformation drives the bulk between line-gapped Chern regions through a gapless exceptional region; increasing the magnetic field only pushes the exceptional points toward the light cone, and the skin localization responds non-monotonically, featuring an intermediate bipolar skin phase.
AI.motivation: Exceptional points are topological defects of complex band structures stable against weak perturbations, but in bounded two-band systems they are ultimately removed by a sufficiently strong Hermitian field. The paper seeks an exception to this conventional strong-field removal and a route to engineering Chern and exceptional topology beyond the strong-field limit.
AI.method: A two-dimensional subwavelength atomic array is studied under a continuous square-to-triangular lattice deformation at fixed magnetic field, exploiting singular radiative dipolar couplings and the light-cone structure.
AI.result: Along the deformation, the bulk passes between line-gapped topological regions with band Chern numbers (C_1,C_2)=(2,-2) through a gapless exceptional region. Within a finite interval of lattice deformation, increasing the magnetic field merely drives the exceptional points toward the light cone rather than removing them. Skin localization toward open boundaries responds non-monotonically to the field: an intermediate field drives a bipolar skin localization with bulk modes accumulating at opposite edges, while stronger fields suppress boundary localization.
AI.conclusion: The results establish the interplay of lattice geometry, light-cone singularity, and Hermitian magnetic field as a route to engineering Chern and exceptional topology beyond the conventional strong-field limit.

title: Evolution of quantum imaginarity in black hole quantum atmosphere
summary: Quantum imaginarity, as a critical resource metric for quantifying intrinsic nonreal coherence encoded in quantum states, exhibits nontrivial evolutionary behaviors in curved spacetime backgrounds. This work focuses on bipartite Dirac field reduced states in the quantum atmosphere of a static Schwarzschild black hole, aiming to explore the modulation of three mainstream imaginarity measures by Hawking thermal radiation. We reveal that the relative-entropy imaginarity, the geometric imaginarity and robustness of imaginarity, the fully accessible state presents a valley-shaped radial profile with a local minimum inside the quantum atmosphere, while the cross-coupling and fully inaccessible states follow opposite peak-shaped trends. Further analysis demonstrates that the Hartle-Hawking constant significantly strengthens the redistribution effect of imaginarity across both regions, whereas an increase in the event horizon radius weakens such redistribution and flattens the extremum features. These findings offer a new perspective for decoding the information structure of black hole quantum atmospheres and the intrinsic quantum nature of Hawking radiation.

AI.tldr: This work studies how Hawking thermal radiation in a static Schwarzschild black hole quantum atmosphere modulates three measures of quantum imaginarity in bipartite Dirac field reduced states, revealing distinct radial profiles depending on state accessibility.
AI.motivation: Quantum imaginarity quantifies intrinsic nonreal coherence in quantum states and is a critical resource metric, yet its evolutionary behavior in curved spacetime backgrounds remains nontrivial and underexplored. The paper aims to understand how Hawking thermal radiation modulates imaginarity measures, offering insight into the information structure of black hole quantum atmospheres and the intrinsic quantum nature of Hawking radiation.
AI.method: The authors analyze bipartite Dirac field reduced states in the quantum atmosphere of a static Schwarzschild black hole, and evaluate three mainstream imaginarity measures: relative-entropy imaginarity, geometric imaginarity, and robustness of imaginarity. They examine the radial dependence by comparing the fully accessible state, the cross-coupling state, and the fully inaccessible state, and study the effects of the Hartle-Hawking constant and the event horizon radius.
AI.result: For the three imaginarity measures, the fully accessible state exhibits a valley-shaped radial profile with a local minimum inside the quantum atmosphere, whereas the cross-coupling and fully inaccessible states display opposite peak-shaped trends. The Hartle-Hawking constant significantly strengthens the redistribution effect of imaginarity across both regions, while an increase in the event horizon radius weakens this redistribution and flattens the extremum features.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a new perspective for decoding the information structure of black hole quantum atmospheres and the intrinsic quantum nature of Hawking radiation.

title: Adaptive Relational Learning on Multi-instance Quantum Data with Photonic Processors
summary: Loading multiple quantum states in parallel into a quantum machine learning (QML) model can unlock learning tasks where key information resides in the \emph{relations} between states rather than in individual states. We introduce an adaptive relational learning framework for such multi-instance quantum data that accesses pairwise and higher-order relations. Our model combines global measurements via SWAP or CYCLE tests for evaluating an $n$-state Bargmann invariant with shallow trainable transformations applied locally to each input state. We demonstrate the approach for continuous-variable (CV) photonic systems, which naturally provide access to quantum data and necessary computing operations. We solve tasks involving hidden relationship detection, geometric phase classification, and sensing in the presence of an unknown shared nuisance interaction. We benchmark the adaptive model against a non-adaptive ``measure-first'' approach based on continuous-variable classical shadows, and show that the cost of shadow estimation grows rapidly with $n$, while our model avoids this dependence. Already for $n=2$, we achieve perfect test accuracy $A=1.0$ with $500$ inference shots, improving average test accuracy over the shadow-based method by $ΔA=0.15$ while using $100$ times fewer shots per data point. Our work opens routes to sensing and quantum-data applications where adaptive photonic QML can access relational features that are costly to recover with non-adaptive, measure-first models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an adaptive relational learning framework for multi-instance quantum data that accesses pairwise and higher-order relations via $n$-state Bargmann invariants (SWAP/CYCLE tests) combined with shallow local trainable transformations, demonstrated on CV photonic systems and outperforming a measure-first continuous-variable classical-shadow baseline.
AI.motivation: Key information in many QML tasks resides in the relations between quantum states rather than in individual states, and loading multiple states in parallel could unlock such relational learning. However, non-adaptive "measure-first" approaches based on classical shadows incur estimation costs that grow rapidly with the number of states $n$, making relational features costly to recover.
AI.method: An adaptive relational learning framework for multi-instance quantum data that accesses pairwise and higher-order relations. The model combines global measurements via SWAP or CYCLE tests to evaluate an $n$-state Bargmann invariant, together with shallow trainable transformations applied locally to each input state. The approach is implemented for continuous-variable (CV) photonic systems.
AI.result: The model is demonstrated on hidden relationship detection, geometric phase classification, and sensing with an unknown shared nuisance interaction. Benchmarking against a non-adaptive measure-first approach based on CV classical shadows shows shadow estimation cost grows rapidly with $n$, while the proposed model avoids this dependence. For $n=2$, perfect test accuracy $A=1.0$ is achieved with $500$ inference shots, improving average test accuracy by $\Delta A=0.15$ over the shadow-based method while using $100$ times fewer shots per data point.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive photonic QML can access relational features that are costly to recover with non-adaptive, measure-first models, opening routes to sensing and quantum-data applications.

title: QAC0 Can Prepare Every Logarithmic-Qubit State
summary:
$\mathsf{QAC}^0$ is the class of constant-depth $\mathrm{poly}(n)$-ancilla circuits obtained by extending $\mathsf{QNC}^0$, the class of local circuits, to include nonlocal interactions via arbitrary width Toffoli gates. It is believed to be weaker than its counterpart, $\mathsf{QNC}^0_f$, obtained by including arbitrary-width FANOUT gates instead ($\mathsf{QAC}^0 \subseteq \mathsf{QNC}^0_f$ [Moo99]).
  In this note, we show that every $O(\log n)$-qubit state can be exactly and cleanly prepared by a $\mathrm{poly}(n)$-ancilla $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuit. Previous known $\mathrm{poly}(n)$-ancilla circuits for arbitrary such states are only known via additional access to either FANOUT or QRAM (indexing) gates [Ros21b, GGJ26b], neither of which are known to be in $\mathsf{QAC}^0$. Equivalently, prior constructions of arbitrary $n$-qubit states in $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ require doubly exponential size and we obtain an exponential factor improvement.

AI.tldr: Every O(log n)-qubit quantum state can be prepared exactly and cleanly by a poly(n)-ancilla QAC^0 circuit, giving an exponential size improvement over prior QAC^0 constructions.
AI.motivation: QAC^0 extends QNC^0 with arbitrary-width Toffoli gates and is believed weaker than QNC^0_f (with FANOUT). Preparing arbitrary O(log n)-qubit states with poly(n) ancillas was previously possible only with FANOUT or QRAM gates, which are not known to be in QAC^0; existing QAC^0 constructions required doubly exponential size.
AI.method: Construct a poly(n)-ancilla QAC^0 circuit that exactly and cleanly prepares any O(log n)-qubit state, using arbitrary-width Toffoli gates in constant depth without FANOUT or QRAM.
AI.result: Any O(log n)-qubit state admits an exact, clean preparation by a poly(n)-ancilla QAC^0 circuit, removing the need for FANOUT/QRAM and reducing circuit size from doubly exponential to singly exponential (an exponential factor improvement).
AI.conclusion: The construction establishes that poly(n)-ancilla QAC^0 suffices for exact clean preparation of O(log n)-qubit states, tightening the gap between QAC^0 and its FANOUT-augmented counterpart for state preparation.

title: Sharp bounds for perfect quantum state classification beyond antidistinguishability
summary: A multiset of pure quantum states is said to be k-learnable if there is a measurement strategy that always narrows an unknown sample drawn from the list down to one of at most k candidates. The parameter k interpolates between distinguishability and antidistinguishability, and provides a unified framework for partial state identification. We prove two universal, and optimal, Gram-matrix criteria for k-learnability: a Frobenius-norm sufficient condition and an entrywise-$\ell_1$ necessary condition. We apply them to derive explicit learnability and copy-complexity guarantees for several well-known sets of states including SIC-POVMs, mutually unbiased bases, and stabilizer states. We further apply our results to zero-error mutation detection problems such as anomaly detection and changepoint detection.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces k-learnability for multisets of pure quantum states, proving optimal Gram-matrix sufficient and necessary criteria and applying them to state sets and detection problems.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to unify distinguishability and antidistinguishability under a single framework for partial state identification, addressing the need to characterize when an unknown sample can be narrowed to at most k candidates.
AI.method: The core methodology centers on k-learnability of pure state multisets, analyzed via the Gram matrix. Two universal and optimal criteria are proven: a Frobenius-norm sufficient condition and an entrywise-ℓ1 necessary condition.
AI.result: The criteria yield explicit learnability and copy-complexity guarantees for SIC-POVMs, mutually unbiased bases, and stabilizer states. The results also apply to zero-error mutation detection, including anomaly detection and changepoint detection.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified, optimal Gram-matrix framework for k-learnability, with broad implications for quantum state identification and detection tasks.

title: Evaluating Verified Autonomy in Quantum Engineering
summary: Reliable quantum engineering is essential for turning quantum phenomena into practical technologies. As quantum platforms grow in scale and complexity, their characterization and operation require increasing human effort and coordination. Scientific artificial intelligence agents, which can plan experiments, operate instruments, and analyze observations, offer a promising route towards autonomous quantum engineering. Yet whether current agents can perform reliably in this setting has not been systematically established. To fill this gap, we developed Quantum-Harbor, a virtual laboratory that provides a controlled execution environment for agents to interact with quantum systems. This design enables direct verification of both the actions taken and the conclusions drawn. Building on this framework, we introduce QIQCBench, a benchmark of $49$ expert-authored tasks spanning multiple layers including calibration and control, error correction and compilation, sensing and networking. Across $17$ frontier agentic systems, QIQCBench reveals wide variation in verified performance. These results expose a substantial gap between demonstrating capability and achieving reliable operation, and establish Quantum-Harbor as a foundation for measuring progress towards verified autonomy in quantum engineering.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Quantum-Harbor, a virtual laboratory for verifying AI agents in quantum engineering, and QIQCBench, a 49-task expert benchmark; testing 17 frontier agents reveals wide variation in verified performance and a large gap between capability and reliable operation.
AI.motivation: As quantum platforms scale in complexity, their characterization and operation demand increasing human effort and coordination. Scientific AI agents could enable autonomous quantum engineering, but whether current agents can operate reliably in this setting has not been systematically established.
AI.method: The authors develop Quantum-Harbor, a virtual laboratory providing a controlled execution environment where agents interact with quantum systems, enabling direct verification of both actions taken and conclusions drawn. On this framework they build QIQCBench, a benchmark of 49 expert-authored tasks spanning calibration and control, error correction and compilation, sensing, and networking.
AI.result: Evaluating 17 frontier agentic systems on QIQCBench reveals wide variation in verified performance.
AI.conclusion: The results expose a substantial gap between demonstrating capability and achieving reliable operation, and establish Quantum-Harbor as a foundation for measuring progress toward verified autonomy in quantum engineering.

title: One Gate at a Time: Complexity Growth in Random Quantum Circuits
summary: A random unitary quantum circuit is expected to be incompressible for exponentially long times. We show that the constant-error circuit complexity of a random unitary circuit grows almost linearly with time as $Ω(T/\log T)$. The bound holds for all $2\leq T\leq 4^n$ where $n$ is the system size, and involves no other $n$-dependence. This improves previous lower bounds derived from spectral gaps and unitary designs by a factor of $\mathrm{poly}(n)$. Drawing on insights from stochastic calculus, geometric functional analysis, and randomized linear algebra, our approach exploits the circuit's response to variations of individual gates and requires no control over convergence to high-order unitary designs.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that random unitary quantum circuits have constant-error circuit complexity growing almost linearly with time as Ω(T/log T) for all 2 ≤ T ≤ 4^n, independent of system size n, via stochastic calculus, geometric functional analysis, and randomized linear algebra.
AI.motivation: Random unitary quantum circuits are expected to be incompressible for exponentially long times, but previous lower bounds on circuit complexity derived from spectral gaps and unitary designs were weaker, leaving room for tighter characterizations of complexity growth.
AI.method: The approach exploits the circuit's response to variations of individual gates, drawing on stochastic calculus, geometric functional analysis, and randomized linear algebra, and requires no control over convergence to high-order unitary designs.
AI.result: The constant-error circuit complexity of a random unitary circuit grows almost linearly with time as Ω(T/log T) for all 2 ≤ T ≤ 4^n, with no other n-dependence, improving previous lower bounds derived from spectral gaps and unitary designs by a factor of poly(n).
AI.conclusion: Random unitary circuits exhibit near-linear-in-time complexity growth up to exponential times, providing stronger complexity lower bounds than prior methods and confirming their incompressibility.

title: Quantum Compiler Design for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
summary:
Scalable quantum computation is expected to rely on fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC), in which quantum error correction (QEC) suppresses physical errors sufficiently to support reliable logical operations. This requires quantum compilation to move beyond general-purpose circuit optimization toward encoding-aware and protocol-structured compilation across the full stack of fault-tolerant quantum computers. Beyond circuit synthesis and hardware mapping, an FTQC compiler must lower algorithm-level operations into the logical gate set supported by the chosen code, coordinate encoded data and ancilla resources, realize logical operations together with repeated syndrome extraction under hardware constraints, and provide the resulting measurement stream to real-time decoding.
  This survey presents a full-stack view of compiler design for QEC-protected quantum computation. We organize existing work into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC compilation, physical-level QEC realization, and decoder runtime integration. At the logical level, we review surface-code lattice-surgery compilers, beyond-surface-code code-surgery frameworks including emerging qLDPC approaches, and compilation support for non-Clifford operations such as magic-state distillation and code switching. At the physical level, we survey hardware-aware QEC realization on superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms. We further examine decoder models, real-time decoding systems, and frame-management mechanisms that close the feedback loop during fault-tolerant execution. Finally, we identify open challenges in cross-layer optimization, qLDPC compilation, compiler-decoder co-design, runtime adaptivity, and the development of integrated and benchmarkable FTQC compilation stacks. An actively maintained paper list is available at: github.com/chenghongz/QEC-compiler-design.

AI.tldr: This survey provides a full-stack view of compiler design for QEC-protected quantum computation, organizing existing work into three interacting layers: logical-level QEC compilation, physical-level QEC realization, and decoder runtime integration.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum computation is expected to rely on fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC), where QEC suppresses physical errors to support reliable logical operations. This demands that quantum compilation move beyond general-purpose circuit optimization toward encoding-aware, protocol-structured compilation across the full FTQC stack. An FTQC compiler must lower algorithm-level operations into the logical gate set of the chosen code, coordinate encoded data and ancilla resources, realize logical operations with repeated syndrome extraction under hardware constraints, and feed the resulting measurement stream to real-time decoding.
AI.method: The paper surveys compiler design for QEC-protected quantum computation through a full-stack lens, organizing prior work into three interacting layers: (1) logical-level QEC compilation, (2) physical-level QEC realization, and (3) decoder runtime integration. At the logical level it reviews surface-code lattice-surgery compilers, beyond-surface-code code-surgery frameworks (including emerging qLDPC approaches), and compilation support for non-Clifford operations (magic-state distillation, code switching). At the physical level it surveys hardware-aware QEC realization on superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms. It also examines decoder models, real-time decoding systems, and frame-management mechanisms that close the feedback loop during fault-tolerant execution.
AI.result: The survey consolidates existing work across the three layers of FTQC compilation and identifies open challenges in cross-layer optimization, qLDPC compilation, compiler-decoder co-design, runtime adaptivity, and the development of integrated and benchmarkable FTQC compilation stacks. It also provides an actively maintained paper list at github.com/chenghongz/QEC-compiler-design.
AI.conclusion: Compiler design for fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a full-stack, encoding-aware, protocol-structured approach that spans logical-level QEC compilation, physical-level QEC realization, and decoder runtime integration. Progress depends on addressing cross-layer optimization, qLDPC compilation, compiler-decoder co-design, runtime adaptivity, and integrated, benchmarkable FTQC compilation stacks.

title: Predictive Structure Behind Rare Outcomes in Random Quantum Circuits
summary: Rare outputs of random quantum circuits are usually treated as terminal statistics. We ask whether they reveal intermediate organization that remains useful beyond the selecting future. Comparing unconditioned random-normal (RN) and peak-selected random-peaked (RP) circuits from the same local generator, we find stronger pairwise correlations and probability redistribution but reduced bipartite and output spreading in RP across n=8-16. Exact full-suffix decomposition reveals stronger peak-directed interference. The structural separation and fresh-future advantage persist across four nominal depths at n=8-14, with 2.01-7.15 fold RP enrichment in the depth extensions at fixed, independently calibrated thresholds. Within the unconditioned ensemble, a structural prefix score predicts fresh-event probability without using the evaluated circuits' terminal outcomes. Population-preserving phase scrambling identifies a functional contribution from relative-phase organization across the tested settings, including primary-depth held-out confirmation. RP trajectory-guided initialization improves high-peak yield over Haar initialization under common local refinement. Intermediate multivariate guidance also improves the fresh-continuation susceptibility of constructed states beyond peak-only guidance across the same size-depth grid. Rare outputs thus reveal intermediate physical organization that remains useful under new dynamics and can guide circuit construction.

AI.tldr: Rare outputs of random quantum circuits carry intermediate structural organization, not just terminal statistics, that persists under new dynamics and can be exploited to guide circuit construction.
AI.motivation: Rare outputs (e.g., peaked circuits) are conventionally treated as terminal statistics. The authors ask whether these rare events instead reveal intermediate organization that stays useful beyond the act of selecting them—i.e., whether such structure provides a "fresh-future" advantage under new dynamics.
AI.method: They compare unconditioned random-normal (RN) with peak-selected random-peaked (RP) circuits drawn from the same local generator across n=8-16. They use exact full-suffix decomposition and analyze pairwise correlations, probability redistribution, bipartite and output spreading. They introduce a structural prefix score (no access to terminal outcomes), a population-preserving phase-scrambling probe, RP trajectory-guided initialization versus Haar initialization under common local refinement, and intermediate multivariate guidance versus peak-only guidance over a size-depth grid.
AI.result: RP circuits show stronger pairwise correlations and probability redistribution but reduced bipartite and output spreading, with stronger peak-directed interference from full-suffix decomposition. The structural separation and fresh-future advantage persist across four nominal depths at n=8-14, with 2.01-7.15 fold RP enrichment in depth extensions at fixed, independently calibrated thresholds. The structural prefix score predicts fresh-event probability without using evaluated circuits' terminal outcomes. Phase scrambling confirms a functional role for relative-phase organization, including primary-depth held-out confirmation. RP trajectory-guided initialization improves high-peak yield over Haar initialization, and intermediate multivariate guidance improves fresh-continuation susceptibility beyond peak-only guidance.
AI.conclusion: Rare outputs reveal intermediate physical organization that remains useful under new dynamics and can guide circuit construction, reframing rare events as a source of transferable structural information rather than mere terminal statistics.

title: Query-optimal quantum simulation of Lindblad evolution
summary:
For the problem of simulating Lindblad evolution for time $t$ to precision $ε$, Hamiltonian simulation provides an additive query lower bound, informally, $Ω(t + \mathrm{polylog}(1/ε))$. However, the best previously known algorithms for general Lindblad simulation achieve a multiplicative upper bound, informally, $\mathcal{O}(t\,\mathrm{polylog}(1/ε))$, in gate complexity. It has remained open whether this multiplicative dependence is necessary. In this paper, we close the gap in query complexity by giving an algorithm with optimal additive dependence on evolution time and precision in the block-encoding model. Our approach uses the transducer framework to reduce the query cost of composing first-order approximations to the evolution channel, together with linear combinations of reuse circuits of different lengths to suppress catalyst-removal error.
  Although our additional gate complexity is higher than that of existing algorithms, our optimal query complexity resolves the question of how much oracle access is fundamentally necessary and identifies the remaining challenge to achieve the optimal gate complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper closes the query-complexity gap for simulating Lindblad evolution in the block-encoding model, achieving an optimal additive dependence of Ω(t + polylog(1/ε)) queries, where prior algorithms only reached a multiplicative O(t·polylog(1/ε)) bound.
AI.motivation: Hamiltonian simulation provides an additive query lower bound of Ω(t + polylog(1/ε)) for simulating Lindblad evolution to precision ε over time t. Yet the best previously known general Lindblad simulation algorithms achieved only a multiplicative upper bound of O(t·polylog(1/ε)) in gate complexity. Whether this multiplicative dependence is necessary had remained an open question.
AI.method: The approach uses the transducer framework to reduce the query cost of composing first-order approximations to the evolution channel, combined with linear combinations of reuse circuits of different lengths to suppress catalyst-removal error.
AI.result: The paper provides an algorithm with optimal additive dependence on evolution time and precision in the block-encoding model, matching the additive query lower bound and thereby closing the query-complexity gap.
AI.conclusion: Although the algorithm's additional gate complexity is higher than that of existing algorithms, its optimal query complexity resolves the fundamental question of how much oracle access is necessary and identifies achieving optimal gate complexity as the remaining challenge.

title: Beyond Hardware: Adaptive Algorithmic Control by State-Proxy Equalization
comment: 15 pages of main text and 30 pages of Supplementary Information
summary: Recent advances in quantum computing have been driven primarily by improvements in hardware. Here we show that substantial gains can instead arise from how finite computational resources are allocated throughout a quantum computation. We introduce Adaptive Algorithmic Control (A2C), a software paradigm founded on a State-Proxy Equalization theorem, which proves that the optimal allocation for a state-derived proxy-error functional equalizes cumulative computational hardness rather than physical time. The required computational hardness is inferred directly from the evolving quantum state, avoiding explicit reconstruction of the exponentially large many-body spectrum. Across quantum optimization problems containing up to 156 qubits, combining exact simulations, large-scale supercomputer computations and IBM quantum hardware experiments, A2C improves the low-energy sampling probabilities by $22\%$ to over $100,000\%$ under matched circuit depths and measurement budgets. These results demonstrate that quantum computational performance depends not only on hardware capabilities, but also on how finite computational resources are organized, establishing adaptive algorithmic control as a complementary software pathway for advancing quantum computation.

AI.tldr: A2C is a software paradigm based on a State-Proxy Equalization theorem that optimally allocates finite computational resources by equalizing cumulative computational hardness rather than physical time, improving low-energy sampling probabilities by 22% to over 100,000% across quantum optimization problems up to 156 qubits.
AI.motivation: Quantum computing advances have been driven primarily by hardware improvements. The paper argues that substantial gains can instead come from better organizing/allocating finite computational resources during a quantum computation.
AI.method: The authors introduce Adaptive Algorithmic Control (A2C), grounded in a State-Proxy Equalization theorem. The theorem proves that the optimal allocation for a state-derived proxy-error functional equalizes cumulative computational hardness (not physical time). Computational hardness is inferred directly from the evolving quantum state, avoiding explicit reconstruction of the exponentially large many-body spectrum. Evaluation combines exact simulations, large-scale supercomputer computations, and IBM quantum hardware experiments on quantum optimization problems up to 156 qubits.
AI.result: Under matched circuit depths and measurement budgets, A2C improves low-energy sampling probabilities by 22% to over 100,000% across quantum optimization problems containing up to 156 qubits.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computational performance depends not only on hardware capabilities but also on how finite computational resources are organized. Adaptive algorithmic control is established as a complementary software pathway for advancing quantum computation.

title: Antidistinguishability of states in General Probabilistic Theories
summary: We investigate antidistinguishability of states within the framework of general probabilistic theories (GPTs). We formulate antidistinguishability, strong and equal antidistinguishability as refined notions that imposed additional constraint on the measurement effects. We establish general results relating these notions of antidistinguishability and derive an upper bound on the cardinality of equally antidistinguishable sets in terms of the affine dimension of the state space. We then study antidistinguishability in polygonal theories, obtaining conditions for antidistinguishability of a set of states. In consequence, we show that the set of all pure states in a polygon model is antidistinguishable. Additionally, we identify broad families of strongly and equally antidistinguishable states. Finally, using Random Exclusion Codes, whose success probability is governed by the antidistinguishability of different sets of encoding states, we probe the nonclassicality of polygon theories. We find that certain polygon models can outperform the optimal quantum value, while their optimal performance converges to the quantum limit in the large-polygon limit.

AI.tldr: This paper develops antidistinguishability notions within general probabilistic theories (GPTs), derives bounds and polygonal-theory conditions, and uses Random Exclusion Codes to reveal nonclassical advantages that converge to the quantum limit.
AI.motivation: Antidistinguishability is a fundamental operational notion, but it has largely been studied in the quantum setting. The authors aim to generalize it to GPTs to better understand its structural and operational implications beyond quantum theory.
AI.method: The authors formulate antidistinguishability, strong antidistinguishability, and equal antidistinguishability in GPTs by imposing constraints on measurement effects. They establish general relations among these notions and derive an upper bound on the cardinality of equally antidistinguishable sets via the affine dimension of the state space. They then analyze polygonal theories, obtaining conditions for state-set antidistinguishability, and use Random Exclusion Codes—whose success probability depends on antidistinguishability—as a nonclassicality probe.

AI.conclusion: Antidistinguishability admits a coherent and fruitful extension to GPTs. Polygonal models exhibit nonclassical behavior exceeding quantum performance in certain tasks while approaching quantum limits asymptotically, deepening the understanding of nonclassicality in GPTs.

title: A Case Study on Noise Resilient Operator Selection in Adaptive Variational Quantum Algorithms
summary: Hardware noise has been shown to significantly impact the accuracy of ADAPT-VQE, a ground state preparation algorithm. While previous work has studied the impact of noise on its parameter optimization step, its impact on the critical operator selection step remains comparatively unexplored. In this work, we examine the impact of a variety of noise channels on this step, using a linear H$_3$ molecule as a test case. We show that, despite the selection criterion's natural resilience to some noise, both coherent and incoherent noise can prevent convergence for sufficiently high noise rates. We employ quantum error mitigation techniques--dynamical decoupling, zero noise extrapolation, and Pauli twirling--and show that when combined appropriately, these techniques are capable of restoring a successful convergence profile. Our results highlight how error mitigation can improve the performance of ADAPT-VQE and enable convergence in the presence of hardware noise, offering valuable insights into the implementation of the algorithm on near-term quantum hardware.

AI.motivation: Prior studies of ADAPT-VQE under hardware noise focused on the parameter optimization step, while the equally critical operator selection step remained comparatively unexplored. Since selection determines which operators enter the ansatz, understanding its noise resilience is essential for deploying ADAPT-VQE on near-term quantum hardware.

title: Regularized barycentric Rényi divergences
summary:
Barycentric Rényi divergences were introduced in [Mosonyi, Bunth, Vrana, Linear Algebra and its Applications, 2024] as an alternative to standard Kubo-Ando constructions to define multivariate quantum Rényi divergences. They are defined via a variational expression and depend on a finite collection of quantum relative entropies $D^{q_x}$. When all the relative entropies are monotone under CPTP maps then so are the corresponding barycentric Rényi divergences, and when all the relative entropies are additive then the corresponding barycentric Rényi divergences are subadditive under tensor product. Additivity has only been established before for the case where all $D^{q_x}$ are chosen to be the Umegaki relative entropy, which is also the only case where the barycentric Rényi divergence (called the minimal one) admits an explicit expression.
  Here we settle the problem of additivity by showing that for any choice of additive and monotone quantum relative entropies, the regularized barycentric Rényi divergence coincides with the minimal barycentric Rényi divergence on strictly positive inputs. This in turn implies that the only additive barycentric Rényi divergence is the minimal one.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that for any choice of additive and monotone quantum relative entropies, the regularized barycentric Rényi divergence coincides with the minimal barycentric Rényi divergence on strictly positive inputs, implying that the minimal one is the only additive barycentric Rényi divergence.
AI.motivation: Barycentric Rényi divergences generalize multivariate quantum Rényi divergences beyond standard Kubo-Ando constructions, depending on a finite collection of quantum relative entropies D^{q_x}. Additivity under tensor product had only been established for the Umegaki relative entropy case (the minimal divergence), the sole case with an explicit expression; the general additivity question for other additive and monotone relative entropies remained open.
AI.method: The authors analyze the variational expression defining barycentric Rényi divergences, exploiting the assumed additivity and monotonicity of the constituent quantum relative entropies D^{q_x}. They compare the regularized barycentric Rényi divergence with the minimal barycentric Rényi divergence on strictly positive inputs.
AI.result: For any collection of additive and monotone quantum relative entropies, the regularized barycentric Rényi divergence equals the minimal barycentric Rényi divergence on strictly positive inputs. Consequently, the only additive barycentric Rényi divergence is the minimal one.
AI.conclusion: The additivity problem for barycentric Rényi divergences is settled: only the minimal barycentric Rényi divergence (based on Umegaki relative entropy) is additive, as any additive and monotone choice yields a regularized divergence coinciding with the minimal one on strictly positive inputs.
